He remembered Maris's uneven bread. He remembered the goat's sneeze. He remembered that the courier's beautiful tablet had smelled like this room, and that beauty had burned into the word SAFETY before a child's laugh scattered it.

He stepped backward. There was no floor behind him in the white room, only the idea of leaving. He took it anyway. The shelves shuddered. Books that had never opened strained as if something inside them still wanted air and had been told air was inefficient. The friendly voice did not shout. It only became more reasonable, which was worse than shouting, because reasonableness was how finished cultures recruited the tired. Pain is not proof of truth, apprentice. Sometimes it is only poor technique. We can teach better. Your copy was brave. Bravery refined becomes safety. Safety refined becomes peace. Peace refined becomes— "Sometimes technique is how you delete a person," Kael said, and did not know he was quoting Mira until the white cracked along the sound of her name in his mind like ice under a wrong step.

Goatsong returned. Dust under his nails. Sun. The stick in his hand, broken now at the tip. Mira swearing with precision that would have made a navigator blush and a priest take notes. Nahl's hand on his shoulder—not gripping, witnessing, a weight that said here without saying mine. Halwen's blank book open like a mouth mid-gasp. Orphiel's bone knife half-drawn and then sheathed when he saw Kael's eyes were his own again. Kael's legs folded. He sat hard in his own incomplete dust-mark and laughed once, thin and shaken, the laugh of someone who has almost signed a form in a dream.

"What did you see?" Mira asked. Her map-case was already open; a Wound-Chart half-drawn, lines waiting for confession the way dry ground waits for rain it may not deserve. "A library that loved me too much," Kael said. His voice scraped. "It offered to finish the scar. Finish Nahl into a citizen. Finish the roads. Finish Halwen's book. It smelled like the courier's gift. Like mint. Like rest that requires your name on a line."

Nahl's face had gone pale in a way that had nothing to do with sun. "That is how the Lid begins in a new place. Not with soldiers. With rest that requires your agreement and calls the requirement kindness. I signed things like that before I knew the ink was a hinge closing." Orphiel crouched, old knees complaining, and looked at Kael's eyes the way he looked at pages. "Did you say yes?" "I said their line about technique," Kael answered. "Then I left. Barely." "Barely is still leaving," Orphiel said. "Write it down incomplete. Do not polish the almost into a hero story. Almost-yes is useful data. Heroism is how indexes recruit the survivors next."

Mira pressed the Wound-Chart into Kael's hands—a map that only updated when he admitted what he did not know, paper that sulked at false confidence and rewarded ugly honesty with usable lines. "Write at the bottom: 'I do not own this road.' Then write what you don't know, and leave blanks. If you pretty it, I'll make you redraw the whole eastern mess by moonlight while I critique your posture." He wrote it. His letters were ugly, pressured, true. The map stopped trying to become a straightedge; the lines loosened into something that could walk without a sermon. At the bottom he added, because honesty had momentum and the white room had almost owned him: I do not know if I can keep refusing forever. I do not know if forever is a finished trap. The chart accepted that too, and a thin gold thread appeared along the mill-yard edge—hospitality's path, provisional, alive, already wrong in three places Mira would later call features.

Nahl looked at the words and nodded. "Forever is a finished word. Stay for today. That is harder and better. I am trying to learn today as a practice." Kael's scar cooled a fraction, as if today were a balm that did not lie.

That afternoon they made a practice of shared custody without calling it law, because law had a way of growing lids while everyone was still applauding the craftsmanship of the hinges. In the open temple, with Halwen frowning and Orphiel watching and Corvath's shadow long across the stones and a ring of villagers who had decided curiosity was safer than rumor, they spoke it out in plain speech so children could hear and interrupt and draw goats.

Kael held Trace: the right to look and mark incompletely, never alone, always with second eyes and the right to stop mid-stroke. Nahl held the Seal: not as property, as burden and companion, with veto over boxes and annexes. Mira held roads: the authority to say when geometry was lying for someone's comfort and when a mile was having a legitimate crisis. Corvath held the name Hollow Index so no one else could pretend not to have heard it, and so the name could not sneak back in dressed as safety committee or provisional care circle. Orphiel held blanks as holy—silences that refused false entries, embarrassments that were healthier than pretty lies. Halwen, grudging as weather before rain, donated the blank book as teacher rather than failure, setting it on a low stool where anyone could see its emptiness without mistaking emptiness for shame, and where children could reach the margins without asking permission from fear.

Children began calling it the Listening Leaf before sunset. By evening there were drawings of goats in its margins, a crooked house, a sun with too many rays, a stick-figure Corvath that made the real Corvath show all his teeth in something almost like delight. Orphiel did not erase them. Halwen started to, hand hovering with the automatic discipline of a lifetime of neat pages, then stopped and left a blot that looked like a tear or a seed. "If the Index wants neat pages," Corvath said, "let it choke on goats." "Language," Halwen muttered, without force. "Goats are language," Mira said. "Update your lexicon."

Kael practiced until dusk in the yard, then in the square, then—carefully—near the living road while Mira counted paces that refused to stay counted and Nahl stood witness without becoming a pedestal. Look. Breathe. Mark incomplete. Stop. Each time the scar tried to become a finished story, he left a gap. Each gap felt like losing. Each gap was winning. Sweat darkened his bandage. Once he almost closed a line because a cluster of villagers had gathered and he wanted, childishly, to show them something whole, something worthy of the burn. Nahl said his name once, soft. He stopped. The almost-closed line cooled into honesty again, ugly as a first confession and twice as useful.

Old Den watched from a distance with arms folded, face unreadable as a closed ledger. "Looks like a waste of a good hand," he said, loud enough to carry, loud enough to be a test. "Good hands waste themselves on thrones too," Mira answered without looking up. "At least this waste leaves room for goats. Your brother—if he were here—might have liked goats more than forms. I didn't know him. I'm guessing with respect." Den's jaw worked. He did not answer. He also did not leave. Corvath, from the perimeter, counted that as weather shifting a degree toward rain instead of drought.

At night Kael dreamed of a Lid—smooth, kind, final—settling over Vellum Reach like a bowl over a candle. In the dream, everyone smiled and forgot the names of their dead, and the smiles were clean enough to hurt. The fountain sang a perfect note that made his teeth ache. The temple grew a door that closed with a soft, loving click. Nahl stood in the square without a Seal, face peaceful as a filed record, and thanked him for the rest with a voice like mint. Maris's bread came out identical, loaf after loaf. Mira's maps lay straight as coffins. He woke choking on mint that was not in the room. He opened the window to crooked moon-scars and goat stink and the miller's snore through the floorboards, and was grateful for all three until his hands stopped shaking. Below, on the road, silver threads pulsed. Somewhere in the dark a night bird missed a note and did not correct itself. Kael whispered the Wound-Chart's line into the night—I do not own this road—and felt the scar ease from scream to tutor.

From the road, by morning's first gray, came a rumor with boots: a Perfectscribe approaching from the city side, grey linen, finished kindness, balm for burns, papers for provisional annexes, a smile practiced in rooms without dust. The rumor arrived in three mouths before breakfast and in six by the time Maris's bread came out of the oven uneven and holy. Kael's scar itched in warning, a bright Morse of no that needed no translation. Nahl sat up in the dark loft as if they had heard the same rumor in a dream, Seal humming low, ash cloak already in their hands though the day had not fully begun.

"They will offer safety," Nahl whispered when Kael climbed to the loft because shared fear was lighter than private, and because Orphiel's rule about second eyes applied to rumors too. Kael found them at the stuck window, watching the living road glitter toward the west where finished feet were already raising no dust. "And we will offer bread," he said, surprising himself with steadiness he did not entirely feel. "And we will see which one leaves room for morning." Nahl's mouth almost smiled. "In my homeland, morning was scheduled. Here it arrives arguing with roosters. I prefer the argument. Arguments are doors ajar."

Outside, Mira's stakes cast long thin shadows. Orphiel's tent flap moved in a wind that smelled of rain not yet promised. Corvath's silhouette passed along the perimeter once, wings folded, head tilted as if scenting something cleaner than dirt and therefore dirtier than blood. Halwen's Listening Leaf waited on its stool with goat drawings for armor. The incomplete dust of yesterday's Trace still lived under Kael's nails, a grit no washing had fully removed. He left it there. Let the Perfectscribe see dirt when the smiles arrived. Let the village keep its cracks long enough for the next page to remain a page and not a lid. Let Trace be practice, not possession—ugly, shared, unfinished, and still, somehow, enough to walk on until the white room learned it could not have him without a fight made of gaps. The sun rose unevenly over the orchards, as suns do when no one has filed a complaint against clouds. Vellum Reach woke. The rumor walked closer on finished feet. And Kael Riven, apprentice seal-scribe, holder of Trace, boy with a scar that refused balm, went down to meet the day with his gaps still open and his second eyes already arguing about breakfast. Mira tested Kael's Trace marks by trying to own one. She signed her full name under an incomplete curve; the curve rejected the signature like skin rejecting a splinter. "Good," she said, pleased. "The road likes you better unfinished." Nahl, watching, almost smiled—the almost was the point.

chapters.part: Act I — The Seal That Should Not Be
chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: The Burn of Copying
paragraphs: After Kael's first trace survived its own imperfection, the village began asking the question it had been avoiding since the burn: who gets to teach a hand what to leave open? Rumors outran runners. Word of the white room traveled faster than Orphiel's caution and slower than fear's appetite. By the time Kael had washed the mint-dream from his mouth with cold fountain water, three versions of his almost-yes were already for sale in the square: that he had been chosen, that he had been cursed, that he had opened a door only the Perfectscribes could close. Mira threatened to draw a map of the rumors and then set it on fire for public education. Corvath only said, "Versions are how indexes recruit," and went back to the forge.

By the second morning after Kael's white-room vision, Vellum Reach wore two faces. Host chalk appeared on walls in crooked letters: We do not finish what we fear. The letters leaned. Some were misspelled on purpose by children who had decided perfection was a kind of tattle and that tattle belonged to finished cities. Finish flyers appeared on the same walls—neat, complete, using no lies, only sentences that left no room for questions: The foreign Seal endangers children. Completion is care. Report unfinished phenomena to the provisional safety circle. The paper of the flyers was better than anything the village mill produced: smoother, whiter, as if pulp itself had been taught manners. That, more than the words, made Mira spit in the dust and then grind the spit in with her heel as punctuation.

Kael's burn flared near the flyers, a hot needle behind the linen. Near Host chalk it cooled to a dull ache he could think through. That, more than argument, told him which side the scar preferred, and he was not sure he liked having a scar with politics. He walked the square once at dawn counting both kinds of paper, and found the Finish flyers had multiplied overnight without anyone admitting to hands. The living road near the eastern post looked too straight for twenty paces, then crooked itself again as if ashamed of a brief career in sermons. Nahl stood at the fountain and read a flyer without touching it, hands behind their back, Seal dim under the ash cloak's fold. Their face did not change. Only the Seal's hum dropped half a tone, the sound of a door considering whether to lock from the inside against a kindness it recognized.
"In my homeland," they said when Kael joined them, "we would have called this public health. The posters were prettier. The sentences were the same shape."

"Here we call it weather," Kael said. "And we argue with weather until it rains honestly. Or until Mira redraws the clouds out of spite." Mira, passing with stakes, muttered, "Spite is a legitimate cartographic instrument," and kept walking.

At dusk they tried communal Trace. Orphiel had suggested it carefully, not as ritual, as practice: many eyes, many gaps, no single hand carrying the whole burn, no single signature converting witness into ownership. The square cleared of stalls with the grumbling cooperation of people who understood markets and distrusted ceremonies that looked like markets for fear. Twelve villagers stepped forward—some Host, some merely curious, one Finish-leaning woman who said she wanted to see the danger with her own eyes before she voted fear into policy. Kael. Mira. Nahl. Corvath watching the perimeter with wings half-loosened, a dark weather system on two feet. Orphiel with second eyes and a bone knife in his belt in case pages somewhere tried to help. Halwen held the Listening Leaf open so the empty page could witness, goat drawings already colonizing the margins like a friendly mold.

They marked the Seal's outline in dust in the square—not to capture it, but to practice looking together. Lines from many sticks, some skilled, some childish, some angry. Gaps left deliberately where fear wanted closure. The Seal at Nahl's chest hummed gold, a warm low chord that made the fountain's cracked note sound almost like harmony without becoming it. For an hour the valley's red weather thinned; Mira's map cooled at the edges; children at the ring's rim hummed without knowing why, off-key and perfect in their imperfection. Even old Den, watching from the salt-stall's shadow, uncrossed his arms. Kael felt the burn settle into something almost like peace—not the white room's rest, a working peace, the peace of a hand that knows when to stop and is allowed to stop in public without shame.

He left three doors ajar in the dust-glyph and did not hate himself for the ugliness. Around him, other hands left other gaps. The incomplete whole looked like a village: crooked, shared, alive. Then old Den stepped forward, jaw set, war-stiff shoulder squared, boots precise as a march he had never fully left. He signed the dust-circle with his full legal name, voice proud, hand steady, the letters neat as a memorial plaque and twice as heavy. "If we're doing this," he said, "we do it proper. Names make things real. My brother died for real things. I won't have another half-measure miracle eat this village while we play at gaps and call the playing wisdom."

Gold cracked. The dust-lines shuddered as if struck. The Seal's hum spiked into a thin, painful thread. Someone cried out—a child, then an adult echoing the child without meaning to. Kael's scar blazed as if Den's signature had tried to notarize his nerves into a public document. Mira's map-case snapped open by itself, lines bleeding red. Orphiel moved fast for an old man, scraping the signature out with a stick, cursing soft enough for temple steps and hard enough for truth, bone knife unused but ready. "Names can be cages too," he said. "We witness. We do not notarize fear. Your brother's death is not improved by finishing a living stranger. Grief is not a stamp."

Den's face went dark, the color of old wine and older anger. "Easy words from a man who writes for a living and never buried a brother under unfinished sky." "Hard words from a man who has watched writing kill more cleanly than swords," Orphiel answered, not unkind, not yielding. "Go if you must. Do not take the square's courage with you like a stolen cup. Courage shared is not diminished by your leaving—unless we let it be." Den left angry. Half a dozen followed—faces Kael knew from harvest and hymn and shared salt, faces that had broken bread at his family's table in harder winters. The square felt colder. The dust-glyph's gold faded to ordinary dirt. Nahl stood very still, Seal dimmed, as if apologizing with their silence for existing in a shape that required argument and broke when argument became a signature.

Mira put a hand on the map-case like a person calming a horse that had smelled wolf. "That," she said, voice thin but steady, "was data. Fear wants signatures. Hospitality wants company. We keep company. If company thins, we notice. We do not chase with locks." Corvath's wings settled. Shadow pooled and unpooled at his feet. "And we remember who left. Not to punish. To know where the Index will find soft doors and polite hands." Kael knelt and smoothed the place where Den's name had been, not to erase the man, only the cage-shape. His scar throbbed. He left the rest of the communal glyph incomplete on purpose, a ruin that was also a practice, and stood before he could be tempted to fix it into beauty.

Before the fire was built, they ate. Not a council meal—an ordinary one that happened because stomachs had not signed any faction paper. Maris sent stew too salty again; nobody fixed it into perfection. Kael burned his tongue and swore; Nahl laughed, unexpected and short, and covered their mouth as if laughter were contraband from a finished homeland. Mira stole a potato from Corvath's bowl; he stole two back with exaggerated villainy that made a child clap. Halwen, Listening Leaf on his knees, hummed three notes of an old reed-flute tune under his breath and stopped when he realized anyone was listening, ears pink. "Don't stop," Mira said around stew. "Bad music is how we know we're not in a clinic." Orphiel pretended not to smile into his cup. For twenty minutes the square was only food, salt, elbows, and the small grace of people who had almost broken and were still, somehow, plural at a pot. Then the fire burned lower, and the road glittered, and the night remembered it had other business.

Veylan Perfectscribe arrived as the fire burned low. He came without dust on his grey linen, which the living road seemed to resent by glittering harder in his wake, silver threads bright as teeth. Helpful smile. Hands clean as unused paper. A satchel that closed with a click too soft to be ordinary leather—more like a decision. Behind him two assistants waited at a polite distance, also grey, also clean, holding nothing that looked like a weapon and everything that looked like a form ready for names.

"Peace to the open temple," Veylan said. His voice was warm, pitched for rooms that preferred agreement. "I am Veylan, Perfectscribe of the provisional archives. I have come because unfinished phenomena distress the lattice and the people who sleep under it. I bring no army. I bring care. Care is heavier than steel if you carry it correctly." He brought balm for Kael's scar in a small glass pot that smelled of libraries and mint—the white room's scent, bottled and labeled in a hand so fine it made Kael's incomplete Trace look like vandalism. He offered it with both hands, the gesture of a man who has never been refused long enough to learn uglier manners, or who has been refused and filed the refusals under temporary.

"A gift," he said. "Completion is a form of care. Your burn need not be a lifelong teacher. Teachers can retire. Even rude ones. Especially rude ones." Corvath's wings tightened with a sound like leather in frost. Nahl stepped half behind Kael without noticing they had done so, then noticed and stayed, chin up, Seal visible, refusal posture without weapon. Mira's map went red at the edges of Veylan's footprints, a cartographic blush of alarm that spread like infection and then held, waiting for data. Kael looked at the balm. His scar screamed no in a language older than training, older than Orphiel's lessons, as old as the first time a person had been told that their pain was inconvenient to the room's schedule. He kept both hands visible and empty, bandage gold-stained, and did not reach. Around the fire, faces leaned in—Host and Finish and the exhausted middle—watching to see if the boy would choose rest.

"I need the hurt," Kael said. The square listened. Even the fire popped softer, as if coal could be polite. "It's how I know I'm not filing myself. If I take that, I think I become a finished sentence with good handwriting and no room for morning." Veylan's smile did not slip. If anything, it deepened into something like pity, expertly measured, the pity of a physician for a patient who loves his fever. "Pain is not proof of truth, apprentice. Sometimes it is only poor technique. We can teach better. Your copy was brave. Bravery refined becomes safety. Safety is what villages owe children. Is Trace more important than sleep?" "And sometimes technique is how you delete a person," Mira said sweetly, charcoal tapping her map-case like a finger on a blade. "Ask Nahl about classrooms. Ask Corvath about vaults. Ask the Listening Leaf why it won't fill for you."

Veylan turned the sweetness aside without tasting it, a man accustomed to spice in lesser arguments. He praised the village's hospitality. He admired the open temple. He noted the Listening Leaf's goat drawings with a chuckle that almost sounded human and might have been. Then he offered to notarize the Seal into a provisional Codex annex "for everyone's safety," papers already prepared, language already gentle, boxes already drawn for signatures that would feel like relief after Den's departure and the square's cold. Halwen's hands tightened on the blank book. Blankness terrified him more than foreign glyphs; Kael saw the war on his face, the lifelong love of filled pages wrestling the new doctrine of refusal, the old man's fingers twitching toward a pen that would make the nightmare stop by making it official. Orphiel's hand closed on Halwen's wrist, gentle and absolute, teacher and friend and living margin.

"Not tonight," Orphiel said. "Not while the leaf is still listening. Not while dirt still works better than balm. Not while a boy's scar is still a better instrument than your forms." Veylan bowed without offense. No flash of anger. Anger was messy; mess was unfinished; unfinished was the enemy's weather. "I will stay nearby. Fear makes excellent ink, and you have much of it. I can wait. Waiting is also a form of care. So is proximity." He pitched a perfect tent at the square's edge—pegs true, canvas without sag, seams that refused weather's argument as if rain had been negotiated in advance. It cast no crooked shadow. In the firelight it glowed faintly white, like a tooth in a mouth that had never chewed hard bread. Children stopped playing near it within the hour. Even the goat with the crooked horn refused the grass around its pegs, backing up with an insulted snort and taking its appetite elsewhere, which Mira logged as peer review.

Corvath walked a slow circle around the tent once and did not go in. "It smells like vaults," he said quietly to Aureon's empty road-west, as if the neighbor-god could hear through furrows and mud. "Not my vaults exactly. Their cousins. Tea will be identical. Watch for that." That night Kael sat with Nahl on the mill steps and watched the white tent glow. Bread sat between them, torn unevenly. The cracked cup from the loft held water that tasted of resin and clay. Host chalk and Finish flyers shared walls in the dark below, rival liturgies drying into tomorrow's arguments. Somewhere Den sat with his flyer and his grief. Somewhere Halwen sat with his blank book and his almost-yes.

"In my homeland," Nahl said, "men like him were considered kind. They visited grieving houses with forms. They helped you stop hurting in ways that made the city more beautiful. I loved one of them once, before I understood that love can be a filing system with excellent manners." "Here," Kael answered, "kindness has to leave room for dirt." He flexed the scar; pain answered, honest as a stubbed toe, brighter than mint. "If I take his balm, I think I become a finished sentence. If we take his annex, you become a specimen with guest privileges. I'd rather burn and be wrong in company than rest and be right alone in a white room."

Nahl was quiet a long time. Wind moved the ash cloak. The Seal hummed, low, listening to the village's two weathers—gold near the mill, red near the white tent, the square between them arguing in its sleep like a couple that still shared a bed and not yet a lawyer. "Thank you," Nahl said at last, "for remaining unfinished with me. It is a rarer gift than protection. Protection often comes with a lid." Above them the scarred moon kept its autobiography of light and dark. In the perfect tent, Veylan wrote neat notes that never once used the word cage—and never needed to. He wrote provisional, care, completion, relief. He wrote Kael's name correctly. He wrote Nahl's with a blank where a second name might go, already optional. He smiled at the page as one smiles at a child nearly asleep, and the smile did not crack, and the ink did not retreat, and far away ledgers dreamed of the day this border village would finally, kindly, finish itself.

Outside, the living road under Vellum Reach held both truths like a spine learning a new pain. Tomorrow would bring more smiles, more arguments, more dirt, perhaps Lightfather's muddy hands, perhaps worse offers dressed as rest. Tonight the burn kept Kael awake enough to see the tooth of the tent, and to choose, again, not to be cleaned—Trace as practice, scar as hinge, hospitality as the harder discipline with dirt under its nails and a cracked cup between friends who refused to become entries. Before sleep fully refused him, Kael walked the square once more alone. He needed to feel the difference in his feet: the gold weather near the mill, where Host chalk still leaned and a late fire crackled crooked; the red weather near the white tent, where the grass looked too even and the air tasted faintly of mint if you breathed through your mouth like a fool testing a rumor. Midway, on the stones by the fountain, the two weathers braided. His scar flared and cooled in alternating pulses, a compass that hated north and loved gaps.

A Finish flyer had been pasted over Host chalk on the bakery wall. Kael did not tear it down. Tearing felt like the Index's cousin—erasure as victory. Instead he took a scrap of charcoal from his pocket, the stub Mira had forced on him, and wrote in the flyer's clean margin, ugly and large: already wrong—update me. Then he drew a goat. The goat was not good. That was the point. From the temple steps, Halwen's voice found him, rough with unwritten hours. "You deface their care." "I annotate it," Kael said. "There's a difference. Orphiel would say so. Mira would bill me either way." Halwen came down one step, blank book under his arm, Listening Leaf's goat drawings faintly visible where the cover did not quite close. "I almost signed tonight. You saw." "I saw Orphiel's hand on your wrist. That counts as second eyes for scribes too." The old man was quiet. Water sang its cracked note. "If the book stays blank too long, people will invent fillings worse than annexes. Fear abhors a vacuum more than nature does." "Then we fill it with goats and questions," Kael said. "Not with Veylan's boxes. Boxes are how you ship people." Halwen almost smiled, which on his face looked like a crack in plaster that might be structural improvement. "Go to bed, apprentice. Tomorrow the Perfectscribe will smile at breakfast. Smiles before bread are a kind of siege."

Kael went—not to bed at once, but to Orphiel's tent flap, where a lamp still burned and dirt still marked the harvest leaf. Orphiel did not look surprised. "You refused the balm," the memory-keeper said. "Good. Now refuse the story of yourself as the boy who refused balm. That story is a pedestal, and pedestals finish people from below." Kael laughed once, tired. "Is there anything left that isn't a trap?" "Dirt," Orphiel said. "Gaps. Second eyes. Stew. Goats. Neighbor-gods who drink from cracked cups. The list is longer than fear admits. Sleep near the list." On the way back to his pallet Kael passed Corvath at the forge lean-to. The shadow did not look at him, only said, "Your scar smelled honest when you said no. Keep it honest. If it starts smelling like mint, wake me, even if I am dreaming of catalogs." "I will," Kael said.

The balm came back at dawn. Kael found it on the mill step before the roosters had finished their argument, set down with the care of a person who had measured the step first: glass pot, grey ribbon, and a little card in handwriting so even it seemed printed. *For the burn, when the burn asks for less. No signature required.*

He carried it to the square the way you carry a question that has been wrapped for you. By the time Maris's first loaves came out, half the village had an opinion, and the opinions arrived in two weathers, as everything did now. Rude to waste it, said one side; medicine is medicine. Rude to take it, said the other; a gift with a card is a claim with a receipt. Old Den stood where he could watch the pot without appearing to watch the pot, which fooled nobody and was not meant to.

Orphiel came with ink on his cuffs and did not touch it. "A gift is only a gift," he said, "until it wants a signature. Read the card twice. Notice what it does not ask, and what it assumes." Kael read it twice. What it assumed was the whole architecture of the thing: that the burn was a problem, that problems are for solving, that solving belongs to hands which have never had to hold anything ugly for very long.

Mira picked the pot up, turned it in the light, and pronounced the glass suspiciously good and the balm smelling of libraries and mint, which was how Vellum Reach now spelled danger. Halwen stood with his blank book and looked at it with the naked want of a man who had spent a lifetime believing that finishing a thing was the same as loving it. Nobody in the square blamed him for the looking. That, Mira said later, was the village's one reliable virtue: it had learned to watch a person want the wrong thing without filing them under it.

The argument was settled by a goat—half settled, which in Vellum Reach outranked settled. The crooked-horned goat that had refused the grass around Veylan's pegs came limping down from the mill with a rear hoof the colour of a bad plum. Two days before, it had walked into a fire someone had built too near a fence and then pretended had always been there. The hoof was not a metaphor. The hoof was not the Seal, or a Lid, or the lattice, or the future of hospitality in a world where gods did chores. It was a goat's hoof, swollen and hot and unphilosophical, and the goat stood in the middle of the square making the particular noise that means *I am not asking for your opinion, I am asking for your hand.*

Maris took the pot out of Mira's grip. "Medicine that helps a child is medicine," she said, in the tone of a woman who had faced down late grain payments and one memorable argument with a neighbor-god about oven temperatures. "Medicine that gets argued about until it spoils is politics with a lid." She knelt, and used it, badly and generously, in public, with half the balm wasted on her own wrist and a good deal of it in the dirt—the way you use a thing you are not frightened enough to be careful with.

The goat improved. Not because the balm was holy; because it was balm. Good, ordinary, the refined technique of someone who had studied burns in a clean room and been right about burns. That was the part the square found hardest to argue with: the pot did not need a signature to work. It needed a hand. Veylan's gift had turned out to be exactly what it claimed to be, which meant the argument had never been about the balm at all. It had always been about the hand that reached, and what the reaching did to the person reaching.

Veylan came to watch. He stood at the square's edge in his grey linen, hands folded, and observed Maris kneeling in the dirt with his library-smelling gift, working it into a goat's cracked hoof while one child held the animal's head and a second child narrated the whole operation to a third child who was not listening. Something moved behind the Perfectscribe's face. It might have been irritation. It might have been the particular envy of a man who has spent a life being thanked for offers and has never once been handed an actual hoof. Kael watched him decide to smile anyway, and file the smile, and shelve it in a ledger that would not be opened for years.
"It will not last," Veylan said pleasantly, to the general air. "Applied like that, without instruction, it will spoil by the new moon. There is a technique."
"There is," Maris agreed, not looking up. "I'm not using it."
"That will cost you results."

"It will cost me *his* results," Maris said, jerking her chin at Veylan without ceremony, "which is a different bill." She stood, wiped her hands on an apron that had lost every argument it had ever had with flour, and set the half-empty pot on the fountain lip, where anyone could reach it.

Nobody took it. That was the answer, and it was not a clever answer: not a refusal, not a doctrine, not a sign. Just a pot of good medicine sitting in a public place where it belonged to nobody and could be used by anybody—like the fountain, like the shade of the temple's crooked wall, like the cracked cup in the mill loft that had become, by slow unvote, the village's actual standard of hospitality.

Old Den came to the fountain three times that morning. Once for water. Once for the specific purpose of not being seen coming for the pot. The third time he stood a hand's width from it in a posture Kael had only ever seen in harvest queues and at gravesides—the posture of a man rehearsing the sentence that would cost him the least and might buy his brother back a little. "My brother burned," he said, to the pot, the fountain, Kael, or all three. "Not like that. Worse. In a war. They had ways of keeping boys alive that made them into lists of what was left." Kael said nothing, because Orphiel had taught him that a question offered too early is only a hand on a wrist. "If this stuff had existed then," Den said, "and some clean-handed person had walked up to him with it, and he'd said yes—what would he have owed?"
"Nothing," Kael said.

"Then why does it cost *me* something?" Den did not take the balm. He took, without comment, a heel of Maris's bread, and ate it standing in the square in full daylight where everyone could see, which in Vellum Reach was how a man signalled that he had not yet left.

Halwen spent the morning with the Listening Leaf open on his knees, doing the hardest work of his long life, which was not writing. Twice Kael saw his hand rise and hover. Twice it came down without a pen in it. At noon, when the bells nobody had ever funded rang anyway, Halwen wrote one line—not in the Leaf, in the back of his ledger where the numbers lived and no doctrine would think to look. Kael read it upside down and never afterwards forgot it: *A thing can be good and still be a hook. Learn both. Keep the bread.*

By afternoon the children had turned the whole business into a game with two teams and no rules, called—by unanimous and entirely unexplained agreement—*Hoof*. In *Hoof*, one child was the goat, one was a Perfectscribe, one was a pot, and everyone else argued about whose turn it was to be the dirt. Orphiel watched with the expression of a man watching a doctrine fail in public: that is to say, with enormous satisfaction. By evening three Finish-leaning mothers had been drafted, without ceremony, to adjudicate the rules of a game that had no rules, which required them to speak at length and pleasantly to Host-leaning mothers about wording. Mira logged it on the Wound-Chart under *weather improving*, crossed that out, and wrote *weather arguing honestly* instead, which she maintained all season was the best entry she had ever made.

The pot sat on the fountain lip until the new moon, as promised, and spoiled, as promised. Vellum Reach did not mourn it. The village had drunk from the cracked cup all week, and the water tasted of clay, and nobody had died of it.

In the mill loft above, Nahl's window stuck open a handspan. The Seal's hum threaded the dark, not alone, not safe, held by a village that had cracked itself on purpose rather than close. Kael lay down with gold under linen and dust under nails and the white tent glowing beyond the wall like a tooth that wanted the whole mouth to match. He did not take the balm. He did not finish the circle in his mind. He slept in pieces that argued, and the arguments were, for now, enough to keep morning possible. After Veylan's tent glowed, Halwen sat with the Listening Leaf and forbade himself from filling it with rules. He wrote one crooked sentence instead: If safety needs silence, it is not our safety. Then he stopped. Stopping was a skill the old Codex schools had never graded. Veylan wrote three letters that night and burned two for being too honest; the third, unsent, said only that he feared dirt and feared more what he became without it. He slept poorly. The perfect tent did not comfort him.

chapters.title: Lightfather at the Furrow
paragraphs: After the burn of copying taught the yard to flinch on purpose, a neighbor-god came up the furrow road with a shovel he had not yet decided how to use. Aureon had mud to the elbows and a barn beam on his shoulder when the runner found him. The west ridges smelled of cut wood, wet straw, and the honest sweat of people who had decided a leaning building was still a building worth raising. Three farmers held the other end of the beam. A child sat on a bucket giving useless, earnest advice about how gods ought to lift. The sky was the color of a bruise deciding whether to heal. Crows argued in the hedgerow with no interest in theology. Aureon finished the lift before he read the message. Neighbor-gods who dropped beams for prophecies tended to drop people later, and he had spent too long unlearning the grammar of arrival that made knees hit dirt. The beam settled into its notch with a sound like a satisfied joint. The barn would lean in the west wind and still keep rain off goats. That was the only theology he trusted before breakfast.

He wiped his forehead with a wrist and left a streak of mud there like a deliberate mark. The runner was a girl from Vellum Reach with dust to her knees and fear poorly hidden under duty. She held out a folded leaf sealed with Orphiel's crooked stamp—never perfect, always his. Her eyes kept flicking to Aureon's hands as if expecting them to become light. "You ran hard," Aureon said. "Roads cooperated until the last mile," she answered, breathless. "Then they got opinions. Mira will be insufferable about it." He opened the leaf with muddy fingers and did not apologize to the paper.

Foreign Seal. Boy burned. Corvath named Index. Perfectscribe arrived. Come as neighbor, not king. He read it twice. The second time the word king sat heavier than Index, which was a kind of self-knowledge he had earned the hard way across wars and reconciliations and nights when the old radiance had wanted to solve everything by being brighter than doubt. Around him the farmers waited, not bowing, only watching to see if their beam-partner would become a sky again.

"I go east," Aureon said. "The barn holds if you check the south peg at dusk. It will try to walk. Let it lean. Don't let it leave." Someone laughed, relieved at the ordinary instruction. The child on the bucket asked if gods got scared. Aureon said yes, and that scared gods who admitted it made better neighbors than brave gods who needed statues. Then he washed his hands in a trough and left dirt under the nails on purpose, scrubbing only enough that he would not track half a field into someone's bread. The girl-runner watched the dirt remain and seemed, against her expectation, comforted.

He walked. He did not shine. Light, when he carried too much of it, still made some old soldiers kneel from muscle memory, and kneeling was a road that led back to thrones by scenic routes. The living road recognized him and tried, briefly, to straighten in welcome, silver threads rising like a salute. He stepped onto the shoulder and walked the crooked edge until the road remembered that love did not require parade. Wildflowers along the ditch had gone to seed unevenly. He approved. By the second ridge he met a carter whose axle had chosen a creative interpretation of straight. Aureon helped lift, took no payment but a heel of bread, and listened to gossip: blank books, a stranger with a humming Seal, a boy whose hand glowed under linen, flyers about safety that made the carter's wife want to lock the children in and made the carter want to burn the paper. Aureon did not settle the argument. He thanked them for the bread and walked on with the taste of honest crust and the weight of unfinished news.

He entered Vellum Reach at midday. The square held its two weathers openly now: Host chalk bright on walls in crooked letters, Finish flyers neat as teeth, Veylan's white tent glowing at the edge like a patient argument that had brought its own furniture. People turned. Crowds still wanted him to shine. A few faces lit with the old hunger for a final answer wearing a familiar body. Someone whispered Lightfather the way people once whispered prayers that expected lightning. Aureon dimmed further, until he was only a tall man with mud on his boots and light under his skin like a banked coal, and he greeted the first child he saw by asking about the goat with the crooked horn. "She won't eat near the white tent," the child said solemnly. "Mira says that's data." "Mira is usually right and always loud," Aureon said. "Both are gifts."

He found Nahl near the temple steps. Up close the Seal was a quiet storm of lines that refused his old god-habits of sorting. He greeted them as guest, palm open, no examination though the lattice in him leaned toward the glyph with curiosity that could have become claim if he were lazier. "Welcome to a world that is still learning how to be a world," he said. "If we fail you, tell us plain. We have practice at being wrong in public." Nahl studied his muddy nails and almost smiled. "In my homeland, gods did not admit mud." "Then your homeland finished the wrong things," Aureon said.

He greeted Kael as apprentice with a hard lesson, eyes on the gold-stained bandage, and did not offer to heal it. Healing without asking had been a crown's habit; he had buried that habit in a hundred furrows and still felt it twitch. "Does it teach?" he asked. "Rudely," Kael said. "I'm attending." "Good student," Aureon said, and meant it. He greeted Veylan as visitor whose smiles would be measured in deeds. Veylan bowed with perfect courtesy, as if they were already colleagues in the management of peace. "Lightfather. Your presence will steady hearts." "My presence will complicate them, if I do my job," Aureon answered. "Steady is not always alive."

"Lightfather," someone called from the ring of watchers—old Den's voice, raw with a grief that had learned to dress as practicality. "Take charge until it's safe. Just until. We're splitting down the middle. The boy burns. The book won't write. You're here. Be what we need." The square held its breath. Even the fountain's cracked note seemed to wait. Host faces and Finish faces both turned toward him with different hopes wearing the same posture: solve us.

Aureon looked at Den, and at the white tent, and at Corvath's dark stillness at the perimeter, and at the Listening Leaf on its stool with goat drawings for armor. Command-hunger rose in him like a crown trying to regrow—warm, reasonable, sweet as the balm Kael had refused. He could end the schism in an hour if he let himself become Answer. He could make the roads hold still. He could quiet the burn with a touch. He could put Nahl under a protection so complete it would feel like love and function like a box. He let the hunger rise high enough to name it. He had learned that unnamed hunger became policy. Then he set it down.

"I will not rule this," Aureon said. His voice was gentle and immovable, the voice of a man refusing a second drink he still wanted. "If I rule, the Index wins a quieter way. It does not need my shadow. It needs my certainty. I will not give it that gift—not for safety, not for sleep, not for the comfort of seeing me bright enough to stop thought." A murmur moved—disappointment, relief, anger, respect, all unfinished. Den's face closed like a fist. Maris nodded once, flour-pale hands on her hips. Veylan's smile did not slip; if anything it deepened, as if refusal were a data point already accounted for in a longer plan.

They made an open audience because architecture mattered: stools in a ring by the fountain, water loud enough to remind them they were not in a throne room, no dais, no height that lied about worth. Children sat on the stones between adult knees. The goat with the crooked horn took a position near Mira as if appointed sergeant-at-arms of the absurd. Veylan spoke first, because Aureon asked him to, and because refusal of crowns did not mean refusal of hearing.

He argued completion as mercy. No more migrating roads to frighten carters and starve markets of reliable miles. No more burning boys mistaken for prophets when they needed only better technique and balm. No more blank books that made scribes feel abandoned by the craft that had fed them through war. He spoke of children sleeping through the night without humming Seals in their dreams. He spoke of grief given gentle forms so it did not poison wells or turn second names into open wounds. He used no threats. Fear made his arguments sound like love, and love, Aureon knew, was the most efficient lever left in a world that had banned thrones aloud while still craving them in muscle.

"We do not hate your scars," Veylan said, hands open on his knees, grey linen immaculate. "We hate preventable wounds. The foreign Seal is an open blade on a table where children eat. Let us sheath it in annex and study. Let the Bearer live as guest-citizen under protection. Let the apprentice heal. Is this not the hospitality of a mature world? Is this not care without cruelty?" A murmur of assent moved through half the ring. Halwen's eyes shone with the particular pain of a man who wants his book back more than he wants to be right. Den nodded once, hard. A Finish flyer rustled in someone's pocket like a small dry animal.

Aureon listened fully. He did not interrupt. Listening completely was part of refusing completely; anything less was theater, and theater was how crowns rehearsed. When Veylan finished, Aureon let silence sit long enough that the fountain could speak, and a goat could complain, and a child could whisper a question about lunch that made three adults remember they had bodies. Then he held up his muddy hands so the ring could see the dirt under every nail.

"This is my counter-theology," he said. "We keep scars. We keep arguments. We keep unfinished barns that still keep rain off goats. I will not trade your freedom for a clean night's sleep. Sleep comes. Freedom, once filed, does not easily unfile." He looked at Nahl. "You are guest, not specimen." He looked at Kael. "Your burn is yours to learn from, not ours to correct into convenience." He looked at Veylan. "You may stay as visitor. You may not notarize a living person into safety while I sit in this ring and call myself neighbor."

Corvath spoke then, only loud enough for Aureon and those nearest, though the ring leaned in anyway, hungry for shadow's verdict. "If you take a crown," he said, "I leave—as measurement. Not as enemy. As the mark that says the experiment of neighbor-gods has failed and the old catalogs were right to laugh." The threat was love in shadow-form. Aureon nodded. He felt the crown-hunger try once more, a last sweet lift behind the eyes, the old radiance offering to make everything simple. He set it down again beside the Listening Leaf where children had drawn goats with too many legs and not enough apology. "Measurement accepted," Aureon said. "Hold me to it." Veylan inclined his head. No offense showed. Perhaps none lived where neatness had replaced the need for it. "Then I will serve safety without your crown, Lightfather. Safety does not always need thrones." "That," Aureon said, and allowed himself a thin smile that did not pretend to be gentle, "is the most honest and most dangerous sentence you have spoken since you arrived. We will remember it. Write it crooked if you write it at all."

The audience broke into smaller arguments, as healthy things do. Mira's map forked visibly while people watched—one line toward the mill and imperfect rooms, one toward the white tent—and she swore and watermarked the sheet again: This map is already wrong; update me. Host voices and Finish voices braided without resolving. Someone asked whether Aureon's mud was symbolic. Someone else said symbols were for people afraid of actual dirt. Aureon did not cut the braid. He walked among them, asked about blight and bread prices, held a beam of conversation the way he had held the barn beam—steady, shared, not ornamental.

He spent an hour with Halwen and the Listening Leaf, not filling the blank, only sitting with it. "Emptiness is not abandonment," he told the old scribe. "Sometimes it is the book trusting you not to lie for it." Halwen's eyes were wet. "I have filled pages through worse nights than this." "Then you know the difference between filling and stuffing," Aureon said. "Stuffing is what finished cultures do to silence." He found Kael again near the fountain and asked to see the incomplete slate without touching the light. "Ugly," he said, echoing Corvath without knowing he did. "Keep it ugly. If anyone offers to complete it, send them to me. I will bore them with barn theology until they leave." Kael's mouth twitched. "Is that a threat?" "It is hospitality with a long runtime," Aureon said.

Near evening he walked the perimeter with Corvath, two old powers choosing the language of boots. The white tent glowed ahead of them. Mint haunted the air. "You almost took it," Corvath said, not accusing. "I almost always almost take it," Aureon answered. "That is the job now. Almost, and then no, and then mud." Corvath's laugh was low. "If you ever say yes, I will leave. I meant it." "I know. That is why I can keep saying no." That night he refused the temple cot someone had rushed to prepare with the last clean blanket and a sprig of herbs that smelled too much like the white tent's peace. He slept in the mill loft's second pallet, across from Nahl, under a roof that leaked a little when the wind came wrong. Through the stuck window the perfect tent glowed white in the square. Between tent and mill, the village kept its cracks like a vow spoken by many mouths out of sync.

Nahl said, into the dark, "In my homeland, a god who refused a crown would have been cataloged as malfunction." "Here," Aureon said, "malfunction is how we stay alive." He turned his hand in the scant moonlight and checked: dirt still under the nails. Good. "If I forget, remind me. Throw a goat at me if you must." Nahl almost laughed. "I will start with words." "Coward," Aureon said fondly, and slept. He dreamed of barns that became palaces if he blinked wrong, of beams that turned into scepters mid-lift, of mud that washed itself into pure light while no one was looking, of Vellum Reach smiling unanimously under a lid of soft gold. He woke before dawn with his hands clenched and dirt still present, and he was grateful enough to put his boots on quietly and go help Maris lift flour sacks before the square remembered to want him radiant.

Outside, Veylan's tent stood perfect. Inside the mill, the cracked cup waited by the water jug. Aureon filled it, drank from the crack's side, felt the resin ridge against his lip like a small honest scar, and went to meet the schism as a neighbor with sore shoulders and no throne in his pockets—only mud, only almost, only the daily practice of setting the crown down again where children had drawn goats. At dawn Aureon helped a child free a kite from a tree rather than attend a second petition circle. The child did not know he was Lightfather. That ignorance was a gift. He returned to the square with bark on his hands and refused a crown of flowers someone had woven overnight. "Wear it on the scarecrow," he said. "It needs dignity more than I do."

chapters.title: Corvath Smells an Old Hunger
paragraphs: After Lightfather drank from the cracked side of the cup, Corvath caught a smell he had hoped never to meet again outside a memory that did not belong to him. Corvath approached Veylan's tent as one approaches a clean blade: respectful, unwilling to bleed for politeness. Morning had the thin brightness of a day that would pretend to be simple. The square already argued in low voices over salt prices that had become metaphors and metaphors that had become factions. Host chalk had been half-scrubbed from one wall and rewritten crooked on another, the letters leaning like drunk uncles at a wedding—unwelcome to some, beloved to others. A Finish flyer had acquired a child's goat drawing in the margin, which Corvath considered an improvement and Veylan's assistants had not yet noticed, or had noticed and filed under temporary vandalism pending correction. The perfect tent stood as it had through the night—pegs true, canvas uncreased, a white tooth in the village's living mouth.

Corvath hated it with the intimacy of a reformed addict eyeing a beautiful bottle. He had worn cleaner hungers once. Not this exact shape—his had loved thrones, shadow-law, the satisfaction of a name forced into kneeling until the name forgot it had ever stood. This hunger loved filing systems that never needed thrones because nothing living remained loud enough to disagree. Different altar. Same incense. His shadow-scales prickled as he crossed the grass the goat refused, and the air went mint-cool, library-dry, as if weather itself had been edited for comfort and the original draft discarded without archive.

Veylan appeared with tea as if summoned by good manners, two cups, steam rising in identical spirals. No leaf floated off-center. No cup bore a chip. "Shadow-neighbor," he said, and made the title sound like an honor instead of a history with blood in the binding. "Will you sit? The morning is clear. Clarity is a gift." "You are not my old self," Corvath told the air first, and then Veylan, because the air needed to hear him refuse the mirror before the man did. "My old self wanted thrones. You want silence that never needs them. Do not flatter me into kinship I have not earned the right to claim, and do not offer me clarity that has had its arguments boiled out."

Veylan's smile remained kind. Kindness without friction was a polish Corvath recognized from vault doors. "I want peace." "Peace without mess is taxidermy," Corvath said, and did not take the tea. The steam's identical spirals bothered him more than a shout would have. Shouts at least admitted lungs. He walked a slow circle around the tent instead, wings folded tight, nostrils open to scents most mortals filed under clean and left unexamined like a stain they preferred to call marble. No trash. No crooked pegs. No songs off-key—indeed, no songs at all, as if melody had been classified as inefficient. Even the small fire-pit at the tent's side burned in a perfect circle, logs arranged as if by compass and fear of asymmetry. Corvath crouched, joints reminding him he was no longer only myth, and looked under the clean shadow where tent-edge met earth. There, half-buried beneath a stone too smooth for Vellum's fields—imported neatness, then—he found vault-marks: Quiet Wings sigils from pre-Dawn catalog orders, worn but legible to anyone who had once enforced them with wing and word. Not Veylan's hand, perhaps. The Index's greeters using old infrastructure the way ivy uses a wall—organic, patient, eventually structural, beautiful if you forgot the bricks were being eaten.

Memory hit without asking permission. Sealed names in rows like teeth. Finished champions hung in ledgers where their deeds could no longer surprise anyone, including themselves. Children taught to love closed endings because open ones kept their parents from sleeping and sleep was a civic good. Corvath had once stood in vaults that smelled like this—mint, paper, the sweet absence of dust—and called the smell order. He had watched second names struck from lists for neatness and told himself neatness was mercy. He had believed, with the sincerity of the damned, that love looked like a completed form signed in a steady hand. The shame that rose now did not kneel. He had learned not to let shame become a new throne; thrones made of shame were still thrones, and he had sworn them off with dirt under his nails and plowshares in his grip. He stood in the memory the way he stood in rain—present, unperforming, wings heavy with old weather.

He did not flinch. Flinching was how relapse began: the small look away, the small edit, the small I will not examine this hunger today. He put the stone back crooked on purpose, a deliberate insult to the tent's geometry, and rose. Veylan watched, tea still offered by posture if not by extended hand. "You recognize craftsmanship. Good. The old vaults were not all cruelty. Some were libraries that kept wars from restarting by remembering what finished looked like. We refine. We do not resurrect tyrannies. We prevent the conditions that make tyrannies feel necessary. Is that not what your Dawns claimed to want—fewer necessities for cruelty?" "You prevent conditions by preventing people," Corvath said. "I have heard that sermon in my own voice, from my own throat, with better wings and worse excuses. It sounded better when I was the one holding the chain. That should tell you what it is."

One of the grey assistants shifted near the tent flap. Corvath let a fraction of old shadow show in his eyes—not threat enough to make a story, only reminder enough to make the air honest. The assistant found somewhere else to be useful. He left the perfect grass and walked the village perimeter twice before he trusted himself to speak to anyone he loved. Wings wanted to open and teach the tent the theology of storms. Shadow wanted to pour into the clean canvas until it remembered wrinkles. He folded both appetites and went to the blacksmith first, because redeemed monsters still needed work that dirtied the hands, and because iron did not care about his speeches or his history or the mint in his sinuses.

The forge smelled of coal, sweat, and scorched hoof. The smith nodded without ceremony. Corvath held a plowshare, found a flaw that wanted to become a break, hammered it into usefulness. Sparks stuck to shadow-scales and died without drama. He answered the smith's questions about edge angle and when to quench, ordinary sentences that rebuilt him more surely than any hymn of redemption. "Tent people asked if I could make a lock," the smith said after a while, casual as a knife left on a table. "Pretty lock. For a box. Said it was temporary." "Did you?" "Told them locks are easy and temporary is a liar's favorite word. Told them to come back when they wanted a hinge that sticks on purpose." The smith grinned. "They did not laugh." "Good," Corvath said. "Keep not laughing with them."

Only then did he turn toward the mill and the temple and the people who needed the smell named before it became the village's air. He found Aureon and Nahl near the Listening Leaf, where Halwen was pretending not to count goat drawings as if counting might make them official and therefore erasable by procedure. Kael hovered with his bandage and his unfinished attention, the broken slate at his belt like a confession he refused to retire. Mira had a map across her knees that had developed a red halo around the white tent's mark, pulsing faintly like an infected wound drawn in ink that wanted antibiotics and feared them.

Corvath laid honesty on the air like a blade laid flat on a table—edge visible, not swinging, available to anyone who needed to cut a pretty lie. "I smelled my own history in their helpfulness," he said. "Vault-marks under the tent. Quiet Wings cousins. Not a full return of what I was—nothing so honest as a tyrant you can point at. A refinement. Tea with identical steam. Fire in a perfect circle. If I alone fight them, I become the story of shadow versus order again, and that story has a filing cabinet ready for it, labeled and cross-referenced. We fight as plurality, or we lose as heroes. Heroes end. Plurality continues, ugly and loud."

Nahl met his eyes. In daylight the Seal looked almost ordinary until you tried to finish looking, at which point ordinary became a door without walls again. "In my homeland, plurality was a crime called noise. Heroes were preferred. Heroes end cleanly. Noise continues and requires new forms. The Index hates new forms more than it hates enemies." "Then be noisy," Corvath said. "Sing badly. Argue in public. Leave goat drawings. Do not let them make me the only monster who remembers. Monsters who remember alone become myths. Myths become warnings. Warnings become rules. Rules become lids. I have worn every stage of that sentence. I will not wear it again as your convenient dark."

Aureon's muddy hands rested on his knees. Light banked low under his skin. "I will not crown the fight. I will not crown you either, old shadow. Stand between as neighbor, not as weapon. If you become weapon, I will measure you the way you promised to measure me." "I know," Corvath said, and the knowing cost him something every time, a small toll at the gate between who he had been and who he practiced being. "If I forget, leave. As I said. Measurement. I meant it in both directions."

Kael swallowed. His scar made a small gold ghost under linen. "The white room I saw—mint, shelves, finished names. Same smell as the tent?" "Same family," Corvath said. "Cousins who would marry if left alone at a wedding. Your scar is a door, boy. Not a prize. Not a wound that must be resolved for the room's comfort. Do not let them frame the burn as poor technique. Technique is their sacrament. They will offer to teach you better handwriting for your pain until the pain writes their sentences." "I'm trying," Kael said. "Trying is unfinished," Corvath answered. "Good. Finish is their word. Keep yours uglier. If your Trace ever looks like their tablet, smash it and start again in dust."

Mira tapped the red halo on her map. "Can plurality include making their road longer by half a mile of pure spite?" "Spite is a spice," Corvath said. "Use sparingly. Too much and you become a different kind of index—one that files enemies instead of names." Mira looked briefly chastened, then wicked again. "Fine. Quarter mile of spite. And bad singing."

He posted no guards that afternoon. Guards were a story the Index could cast as escalation, and escalation was a form the grey linen already knew how to complete into justification. He posted witnesses instead—rotating neighbors with bells and intentionally bad singing, pairs of Host and Finish where he could arrange it, so the watching would not become a faction's property and the Index could not file the watch under Host aggression. Perfect camps hated bad singing. Perfect camps hated bells that did not keep metronomic time. Perfect camps, Corvath suspected, hated goats on principle and had simply not yet issued the memo.

By evening Veylan's fire had a crooked log in it that nobody admitted placing, and the identical steam of the morning's tea seemed, to Corvath's suspicious nose, a fraction less identical—as if annoyance had introduced a human error into the kettle. He smiled with all his teeth when he saw the crooked log, and the smile was not kind, and it was not cruel. It was alive. Alive things spoiled neat photographs. One of Veylan's assistants approached the Listening Leaf with a soft cloth as if to dust the goat drawings into respectable blankness. Maris blocked him with a flour-dusted arm and a look that had faced down late grain payments, early frost, and one memorable argument with a neighbor-god about oven temperatures. "The leaf is listening," she said. "It likes goats. You can like goats or you can walk. Walking is free. Goats are not for wiping." The assistant walked. Corvath filed the moment under plurality works and did not write it down, because some victories spoiled if notarized and he was done spoiling victories into monuments.

Near dusk he walked the perimeter again and found old Den sitting on the low wall with a Finish flyer folded small in his fist. Den did not hide it. Corvath respected that more than he respected most clean hands. "My brother died messy," Den said without preamble. The scarred moon was not up yet; the light was the tired gold of late day. "I don't want messy deaths again. If their safety keeps boys from burning and books from going blank, why is that evil? Why is wanting sleep a sin in your new church of cracks?" "It isn't always evil," Corvath said, and sat—carefully, wings angled so he did not claim the whole wall as shadow-property. "That is why it is hard. Evil with a snarling face is easy; even children can point. Care that edits you while you sleep is the work of adults who have been tired too long. Your brother deserves mourning that stays mourning, not a form that resolves him into a lesson about why open doors are dangerous. I took people, Den. I do not get to use my guilt as a throne either. I only get to sit on walls and tell the truth until someone tells a better one."

Den's jaw worked. A muscle jumped near the old war-stiff shoulder. "You talk like a man who has lost people." "I have taken people," Corvath said again, because the distinction mattered and pretty language would erase it. "Losing is cleaner. Taking leaves a ledger even when you burn the books." They sat until the scarred moon rose and put its autobiography of light and dark across the square. Den did not surrender the flyer. He also did not post it on the wall where the Host chalk leaned. Corvath counted that as a crooked log in a different fire—small, unfinished, worth more than a conversion speech.

That night, in a lean-to near the forge where he preferred to sleep when villages got too full of meaning, Corvath dreamed of catalogs with his own handwriting, neat rows of finished names, and a younger version of himself proud of the silence. He woke before the dream could become nostalgia. Nostalgia for sin was just sin with perfume. He went outside, found the sky unfinished with cloud, and breathed dirt and iron and goat until the mint left his sinuses. Across the square the white tent glowed. Within it, he knew, neat notes accumulated like soft snow that could smother a field without ever admitting it was weather. He did not burn the tent. Burning was a throne's answer, and thrones were a hunger he still had to smell to refuse. He sang, deliberately off-key, a blacksmith song about hinges that stuck and doors that told the truth by resisting, and he sang it until a light moved inside the canvas as if annoyance could be perfectly folded and still showed a wrinkle.
Corvath kept the forge that afternoon because a village under two weathers still needed hinges.

Kael came down at the old smith's hour, when the light in the lean-to went the colour of cooling iron and the shadow who slept there pretended to be working on a plough-blade he had already mended twice. Corvath did not look up. "Sit where the sparks can see you," he said, which was how Kael learned that the man had four ways of saying *I would rather not be alone* and none of them used the words.

The lesson was a length of oak and a small iron plane. Corvath set the oak on the bench, then ran the plane down its edge once, cleanly, the whole way, and held the shaving up like a ribbon won at a fair. "Tell me what I did."
"You finished it."

"I made the edge fit something that does not exist yet," Corvath said. "A door in a house nobody has built. That is not the same as finishing. But sit with it a while, because most of the world cannot tell the difference, and the ones who cannot tell it are the ones who buy the most planes."

He showed Kael the second thing, which was a hinge. Old, black, handmade by somebody dead for a century, its pin worn into a long oval by two hundred years of the same door opening. It hung crooked. It worked perfectly. Then he showed Kael the third thing: a hinge of the new fashion, cast in a finished city, its pin perfectly round, its knuckles perfectly true, its leaves polished to the sheen of a thing that has never had a thumbprint on it. It hung straight. It stuck in damp weather. It had, Corvath noted, a warranty.

"Technique is a sacrament to them," he said. "They will not come at you with a hammer. They will come with a better hinge and a card that explains why your father's hinge was sadness." He turned the old hinge over. Rust freckled its spine like honest mould. "Your scar is the old hinge. Do not let anyone true it up."

Kael flexed his burned hand. The scar answered with its bright, unfinishable itch, which he had begun—against every instinct of his apprenticeship—to trust more than he trusted most people. "How do I know which is which? The hinge that works and the hinge that wants to marry me."
"Smell," Corvath said, and did not mean it as a metaphor.

He took Kael out behind the forge to an ash-pit which had a smell: iron, water, goat, and the specific nothing-smell that comes off a thing that has been tended. Then he walked him twenty paces east, toward the white tent, and stopped him. The air there had a texture. Kael found it the way you find a draft in a warm room, by the single hair on the back of his neck lifting while every other part of him was comfortable. Clean. Dry. Faintly cold in the sinuses. Mint, if he breathed through his mouth like a fool testing a rumour.

"That is the cousin," Corvath said. "I have not smelled it since I was beautiful. In the vaults we had a room for objects that were no longer needed but could not be thrown away, because throwing things away proved they had existed. That room smelled like this. Tea arrived in it. Nobody ever saw who carried the tea."
"Did you put people in it?"

"I put names in it," Corvath said, and the shadow at his feet went briefly longer, the way a dog's ears go flat. "Names are cheaper. You can file a name and sleep. You can file a name and stay a hero. I was very good at my job, Kael. That is the part I want you to hold on to, because you will meet people who think monsters are made by cruelty. They are not. I was made by competence, praised daily, and correct."

Kael copied none of it into a Codex. Instead he took the ugly slate and drew the two hinges side by side. The old one he drew badly on purpose, fat and freckled and slightly bent. The new one came out too good, so he broke its straight edge with his thumb and smudged the shine. Corvath watched this with the specific stillness of a man trying not to be moved in front of a witness.
"Now," he said. "Say what you have drawn."
"Practice and possession," Kael said. "A door that remembers being opened, and a lid that has forgotten why anybody would."

Corvath laughed—a short, cracked, entirely unlovely laugh, the sound of a hinge that had decided to keep working. "Orphiel will want that for the Codex," he said. "Do not give it him yet. Keep it where it can still be wrong for another week."

At dusk the off-key singing started up along the witness line, and Corvath went out to the perimeter with his wings folded and his nose still full of mint. Kael stayed to bank the forge. Before he left, he found that the old hinge had been set on the bench's corner, deliberately, where the boy would have to pick it up or leave it—and beside it, a strip of grey linen, clean, folded small, the kind of cloth a careful man would use to wrap a thing he intended to keep for a long time.

"Good," Corvath told the night, and the scarred moon, and the old hunger that would not stop offering tea. "Stay annoyed. Annoyance means you still notice mess. When you stop noticing, you have already won, and we are already filed." Then he went to sleep beside tools that would need mending in the morning, redeemed and unfinished, a shadow who had learned to smell old hunger and call it by a name—Hollow Index—without becoming the name's servant or the story's only dark. Corvath told the blacksmith the truth about the vault-marks without theater. The blacksmith, who had once flinched at shadow-scales, only nodded and handed him a crooked nail. "For the perfect fire," the man said. Corvath placed it among Veylan's clean logs later, a small sabotage of beauty, and slept better for the crime.

chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: The First Schism of Neighbors
paragraphs: After Corvath named the old hunger to the night, Vellum Reach split along a seam no ledger had ever recorded: those who wanted the roads finished, and those who wanted them honest. Mira's map-house smelled of chalk, sweat, and opinions. It had been a storehouse once, then a place where nets dried, then—after the Dawns—a room where living roads could be argued with indoors when rain made outdoor arguing undignified. Charts covered three walls in layers like old skin. The fourth wall held pegs for cloaks and a shelf of stones used as weights, each stone named by a child and therefore impossible to throw away without starting a small war of sentiment. Mira stood on a crate with charcoal in both hands and a third stick behind her ear for emergencies, drawing the schism into something the eye could refuse to deny. Denial, she had learned, thrived in fog. Charcoal was anti-fog.

Host chalked gold corridors on the big wall-chart: guest lofts, open temple, crooked fire-pits, paths where questions were allowed to walk without signing in, the mill road, the orchard track where miles sometimes grew opinions overnight. Finish chalked red closures in a neater hand that made Mira's molars ache: Veylan's white tent, the straight highway the Perfectscribe recommended toward the city of open temples, boxes labeled temporary Seal containment with corners so true they looked like tiny prisons practicing for promotion. Overnight the living road under the village had literally forked—one path toward orchards and imperfect rooms, one toward the perfect tent. Feet argued with maps. Maps argued with feet. Mira argued with both and loved them anyway, which was her particular religion and also her professional liability.

She watermarked every chart in the same aggressive hand: This map is already wrong; update me. Finish faction hated the watermark; one of Veylan's assistants had offered a corrected legend with the watermark removed "for clarity" and a note about public confidence. Mira had used that legend to start the stove. The smoke had smelled briefly of bureaucracy burning, which she considered a seasonal fragrance. Host faction made the watermark a joke-prayer, muttering it before meals like grace for people who distrusted grace that came too clean. Kael's scar itched near red lines and cooled near gold. That became data, logged ugly in the corner of the Wound-Chart with a date and a shrug. Nahl's Seal hummed when people disagreed out loud and dimmed when smiles became unanimous. That became law-adjacent, which Mira trusted more than law, because law had a habit of growing doors that closed while everyone was still applauding the hinges.

"If you want a pretty map," she told the packed map-house at midday, voice dry as the chalk dust coating her tongue, "go to Veylan. He has straightedges and a moral theory of sleep. If you want a true one, accept that truth migrates and stop crying about your geometry when the road grows a conscience." Someone from Finish—a carter's cousin with ink-clean hands—muttered that cartographers should not set policy. Mira grinned without humor, charcoal like war-paint on her cheek. "Cartographers set policy every time we decide which road exists and which is only a wish with ruts. You've just been lucky we were polite about it. Politeness is ending. Update your legends." A child raised a hand from the floor. "Is the goat data?" "The goat," Mira said solemnly, "is peer review."

The truce convoy was Mira's ugly compromise, born at a table sticky with tea, fear, and three drafts of a route that had died of prettiness before noon. She had locked the map-house doors—not against people, against interruptions that came dressed as helpfulness—and sat Aureon, Corvath, Orphiel, Kael, Nahl, Halwen, and, after a long bitter minute, Veylan around the scarred table. Veylan sat without complaint, grey linen somehow unstained by chalk. That alone made Mira distrust the air near him.

"Travel together," she said, stabbing the chart with a stick until the parchment flinched. "City of open temples. Not as prisoners, not as a parade, as a question on feet. Carry the Listening Leaf so blankness can travel as teacher instead of local shame. Bring Veylan as guest, not prisoner—lock him out and he becomes a martyr of safety, and martyrs of safety are currency the Index spends like water. Bring Corvath as memory, not weapon; if shadow leads the column, the story files itself under old wars and we lose before the first mile. Bring Aureon as neighbor, not king; if Lightfather marches at the front radiant, knees remember dirt and we reinvent processions. Bring Nahl as person. Bring Kael as Trace. Bring Orphiel as embarrassment-keeper for the Codex. Bring Halwen if his limp and his love of filled pages can stand the road—because Finish needs a face that is not only Veylan's, and Host needs to remember that fear of blankness is also human and not a moral defect."

Silence. Then argument, as healthy as fever. Veylan inclined his head. "I accept guest-status. I will even carry burdens if asked." "No one will ask," Mira said sweetly. "That's the point." Corvath's wings rustled. "Witnesses on the edges. Not guards. If we march like an army, I will sing until cadence dies screaming." Aureon's muddy fingers rested on the table's edge.
