In Vellum Reach, far behind the convoy, someone repairing a cracked cup stopped before making the repair invisible and left the seam visible on purpose. In Chordfall, a singer hummed Scar-Interval while washing bowls and did not notice Emberion's dim-bright approval overhead. In the Quiet Wings hills, night air moved through open shafts and smelled less of mint. Veylan, awake on the ridge, felt the non-binding message pass through him like weather he could not annotate. For the first time in many patient years his hand twitched toward a pen and then away. Some documents, even he almost understood, should not be written if writing them completed the wrong thing. The almost passed. Patience returned. Emberion dimmed a fraction over that patience—not curse, report. Corvath stood watch and did not look up at first. Looking up had once been for omens that justified drawers. When he finally raised his face, he saw only pattern: old light, long returns, room braided through brightness by a silence he respected. "Not chain," he said aloud, to the bell, to himself, to the hunger that still sat in his corner like a dog told stay. "You hear that? Not chain."

Aureon, dirt under nails, slept through most of the star-speech and received it as a dream of buckets with holes watering crooked rows. He woke smiling without knowing why. That was acceptable sky-law: kindness that did not require comprehension as entry fee. Kael's scar, in question-mode sleep, wrote one airless letter against his palm and erased it: a hook without eye, incomplete. He did not need to see Emberion to practice constellation law. Shared custody was already star-work at ground level. Mira woke, redrew one kink, and found herself writing in the margin without planning to: Pattern not chain. Chain = pattern − mercy. She stared at the line, snorted, and added her watermark underneath so no one, including her, could pretend the sky had finished the chart.

From constellation height the city of open temples glittered like a question. Many thresholds. No single door. Lanterns unmatched. Somewhere under its friendly streets a Hollow structure rearranged soft rooms and finished smiles, still certain that relief was love and love was closure. Emberion did not smite the Hollow. Smiting would teach the world that endings from above were still the correct language. Instead the dragon-star held pattern: brighten gold, dim red, braid silence, leave dirt sacred, refuse the chain. Serenya's hush deepened along one approach road the convoy would walk at dawn—not blocking, cushioning, making room for doorstop culture to enter without being immediately translated into obsolete. Along the gold kink still cooling from the convoy's passage, night insects sang unresolved phrases. A ridge fox paused under Emberion's brightening and did not become a symbol. It was only a fox. Sky-law that turned every animal into omen was chain-work. Emberion let the fox be fox, the bean be bean, the child-doorstop be child. Meaning could visit without colonizing. In a Quiet Wings shaft, moonlight fell on a soot-mark—HUNGER, NOT PERSON—and the mark did not glow with destiny. It only remained legible to the next tired walker. Remaining was enough. Remaining was pattern. Serenya's silence braided a second time through the light as the convoy slept into the end of their mute day's gifts: doorstop culture settling into muscle, scar-script resting in question-mode, Aureon's almost filed as information not prophecy. Where silence met starlight, a third thing formed that mortals might later call mercy if they were careful not to crown the word—room enough for unfinished people to continue.

The constellation turned as constellations turn: slow, non-binding, older than catalogs. MESSAGE TO EARTH (residual warmth only): You are tired. Tired is not a drawer. Sleep unfinished. Wake plural. Keep the door from slamming with whatever weight you have—bean, bell, child, scar, song, stubborn second name. Emberion's eye half-lidded, not in boredom, in trust that the ground would do what ground does when people keep hospitality as Seal-practice: remain. Crack. Grow. Argue. Hold. The unwritten stayed unwritten on purpose. The stars, for once, approved of the blank. Far below, a child on the ridge woke and pointed at a star without asking it to rule her. Emberion brightened once—not as reward, as recognition of looking without kneeling. The child's mother pulled a blanket higher and did not shush the pointing. Pointing was not catalog. Pointing was relation. In the Quiet Wings vaults still far behind the convoy, dust settled on drawers that had been opened and not re-sealed into perfection. Sky-law noted the dust as honest sediment. Index-law, if it still watched from residual white static, would have called the dust error. Emberion preferred the sediment. Serenya's silence moved along one more road the convoy would walk—cushioning, not blocking. Where silence met starlight, room enough remained for unfinished people to continue without becoming symbols against their will. A fox crossed the gold kink and remained a fox. A bean root found a stone and went around it without filing a complaint. Pattern, not chain. Mercy left in the joints of the world.

chapters.part: Act III — The Road of Living Scars
chapters.label: Chapter 17
chapters.title: Departure with Dirt Still Under Nails
paragraphs: After Interlude B, the inner circle packed for a city of open temples, carrying dirt, bread, and exactly one vow none of them could yet say aloud. They left the ridge without washing their hands. Dawn had the color of old brass. Mist clung to the last campfires the way children cling to a parent who is already standing. Packs creaked. Goats complained in the philosophical tone of animals who have traveled too far and intend to bill the world for it later. Someone laughed once, too sharp, and someone else shushed them without meaning to, and then both of them laughed properly, because shushing had become a joke since the Seal asked for silence and then returned speech like a loan repaid with interest. Nahl flexed their fingers and studied the dark crescents under each nail. Ridge soil. Furrow grit. The signature of a road that had kinked overnight rather than lie straight for anyone's convenience. In the homeland that half-lived behind their eyes, earth on the skin was a demerit, a moral failing written in grit. Here, when a greeter in a white sash stepped from a booth of polished wood and asked for proofs of identity, Corvath held up both palms as if presenting medals.

"Passport," Corvath said. The greeter's smile was the sort of smile that never learned weather. "Clean hands process faster, honored travelers. Automated kindness prefers clarity." "Then process us slowly," Aureon said. He carried no scepter. A farmer at the last camp had lent him a shovel with a cracked handle and a blade that still held yesterday's clay. He rested it across his shoulders like a yoke and looked, for a moment, like any neighbor who had work to do. "We are not in a hurry to become clear." Behind them the ridge camp dissolved into motion: tents collapsing into packs, bread torn and shared, a last look at the place where a day of requested quiet had taught them a vocabulary sturdy enough to walk on. Children practiced being doorstops in the dust, sprawling across imaginary arguments until adults stepped carefully around them and called it training.

Veylan Perfectscribe stood slightly apart, hands already washed in a basin of water so pure it smelled of nothing. The greeters waved him into a gold-lit queue that moved like a dream of efficiency. He glanced back once. Shame flickered across his face—not theater, not strategy, something smaller and more honest—and then the queue took him and his perfect boots left no print on the stone. Kael watched the printless stone and felt his scar itch under its linen. "That's not weather," he murmured to Mira. "That's editing." "Red at the edges," Mira said. She had the Wound-Chart open against her forearm, ink already bleeding gold where the checkpoint's kindness tried to straighten the path. "Gold deeper in. We take the long queue with the dirt."

The long queue smelled of goats and onion and the honest sweat of people who had slept on uneven ground. A child in front of them counted freckles on his sister's arm, lost the count, and started again, delighted by failure. An old woman argued with a clerk about the spelling of a second name the clerk insisted had been "resolved." The old woman won by singing the name wrong on purpose until the clerk's pen refused to finish the stroke. Ink pooled. The form sulked. The queue advanced by inches that felt like life. Nahl stayed three paces from the place where Veylan had vanished into speed. Doorstop distance. Close enough to intervene. Far enough not to be filed as his companion. "You flinch when he is near," Kael said quietly. "I flinch when keys are near," Nahl answered. "He is shaped like a keyhole's dream of a key." Kael's laugh was soft and scarred. He Trace-marked the booth's corner with an incomplete curve that looked like a mistake from a distance and like a question up close. The greeter's smile stuttered. Automated kindness did not know what to do with questions that refused to resolve into identity.

"Name?" the greeter tried again, gentler, as if softness could finish what speed had not. "Nahl," they said. "Bearer only when I choose the word. Guest today." "Affiliation?" "Dirt," Corvath supplied, showing his nails again. "And bad singing. And a god with a shovel. File us under unfinished, if you must file." The greeter's stylus hovered. Somewhere in the booth a crystal chimed a complaint. Then the machine of kindness did the only honest thing left to it: it failed elegantly and waved them through into the longer gold that still moved like people.

Beyond the checkpoint the road widened into a vault-approach of packed earth and memory-stone. Birds crossed the sky in grid patterns—too even, too purposeful, the way scouts fly when they have forgotten they are animals. Their shadows fell in tidy rectangles across the convoy's faces. Harmonix stopped walking and clapped. Not on the beat. Off it. One clap where a hymn would rest, two where a march would breathe, a scatter of palms that made the children giggle and the birds tilt as if the air had become unreliable music. "Again," Harmonix said. "All of you. Break the grid. Grids are how Indexes teach wings to file themselves." The convoy clapped badly. Farmers clapped like men counting seed. Scribes clapped like people embarrassed by joy. Corvath clapped with the heavy pleasure of a redeemed monster discovering rhythm. Aureon's clap was late and sincere. Nahl's hands found a pattern from no homeland—something between goat-bell and heartbeat—and the Seal under their shirt hummed a gold thread that made Kael's scar warm without burning. Sancora clapped with a healer's timing: irregular on purpose, attentive to pain. Orphiel clapped once and then stopped to listen to the echo, as if the air itself might write something true. A Finish faction couple near the rear clapped perfectly on Harmonix's off-beats, which made Harmonix grin like a knife finding butter. "Even opposition can learn mess," she said. "Good. Mess is a civic skill."

The birds broke. First one peeled left into a true flock-curve. Then three. Then the whole sky relearned animal. They became crows and sparrows and a single hawk that had no interest in paperwork. Feathers fell like black confetti. A girl caught one and stuck it in her hair and declared herself a general of nothing. A boy tried to salute and dropped his bread and decided the bread was a better general. "Ugly incompletes," Kael said, Trace-marking the air where the grid had been. Lines of light hung crooked—bird-rests for anything that needed a place to land without being counted. "If they come back neat, we know the Index is rewriting the sky again." "The sky does not like being rewritten," Harmonix said. "Neither do throats. Keep the off-beat in your pocket. If a greeter offers you a metronome, throw it in a well." "That seems wasteful," Veylan said, rejoining them from a side path so clean it looked scrubbed by apology. He had a fresh ledger under his arm. "Metronomes are tools." "So are cages," Corvath said mildly. "I used both. I recommend neither for birds."

Veylan's mouth tightened, then smoothed. "I verified the southern greeters. No harm planned. You invent hostility to justify your theater of mud." "Mud is not theater," Aureon said, and lifted the shovel so the clay on it caught the light. "Mud is what remains when you refuse to sand a life into a diagram." For a stretch they walked without speaking much. The city rose ahead in stacked thresholds and open courts, roofs patched with living green, smoke from real kitchens. Between ridge and gate the air thickened with the particular pressure of a place being argued over by two futures. A cart of cabbages rolled past with a Host faction banner that had been mended so many times it looked like a map of arguments. The driver nodded at Aureon's shovel as at a cousin. Farther on, a Finish family walked the shoulder of the road in clean shoes, children quiet in the way of practiced calm. One child looked at the convoy's off-beat remnants—still clapping under their breath—and smiled a real smile before the parent's hand settled on their shoulder and the smile sanded itself down. Nahl saw it and tasted metal. Kael saw Nahl see it and Trace-marked the air between the child and the convoy with an incomplete curve that meant, if you knew how to read scars, You can find us later. No one owns your mouth. "That mark won't hold against a household Lid," Veylan said, not unkind for once. Observant. "You give children weapons made of chalk and hope." "I give them hooks," Kael said. "Hooks are how you climb out of smooth places."

Sancora fell into step with a woman from Chordfall who had blistered her heels raw on gold paths and refused the red shortcuts anyway. They traded blister stories like medals. Harmonix taught a cluster of teenagers a clap that sounded like error and was design. Corvath told a short, ugly story about a drawer that had once held a name like his, and when he finished no one clapped—they only walked closer to him, which was better applause. The living road under their feet kinked once, gently, as if agreeing that straightness could wait. Mira swore fondly at her chart as the kink ruined a measurement and improved a life. Orphiel walked with the Listening Leaf open against his ribs. Blank pages fluttered as if sniffing the road. "Memory-fields ahead," he said. "I can taste the edits. Someone has been polishing yesterday. The polish smells like milk left too long in a clean cup."

Mira's map bled. Gold veins ran toward the city; red filaments tried to straighten them into avenues. She did not wipe the blood of ink away. "We go through," she said. "Straight is a trap. Pretty is a trap. Anything that promises you will arrive the same person who left is a trap with flowers on it." "Comforting," Kael muttered. "I am a cartographer," Mira said. "Not a lullaby. If you want comfort, ask Sancora for tea that admits it cannot fix everything." "I have that tea," Sancora called from two ranks back. "It tastes like honesty and mint. People hate it, then ask for more." Nahl smiled despite the pressure gathering behind their eyes. "In my schools we had teas that made forgetting sweet. I prefer mint that argues."

The true vault-road mouth opened under the city's southern lip: an arch of living stone that still remembered being a hill. Lichens wrote unfinished essays across its face. Memory-fields shimmered beyond it—streets that recalled wrong on purpose or by Index edit, alleys that insisted they had always been straight, fountains that had forgotten the names of the people who built them and remembered, with unnatural clarity, the hours they had been cleaned. A mural on the inner curve showed the Dawns as neighbors with muddy hands. Someone had tried to repaint the mud into pure light. The living pigment rejected the purity and cracked into honest brown again while they watched. "That's a good omen," Mira said. "Paint with opinions."

Nahl stepped into the first shimmer and saw, for half a breath, a classroom of children erasing their dead with soft white cloths. The vision tasted like metal and milk. Desks aligned. Windows without smudges. A teacher's voice like a warm lid: Grief that lasts is a defect. Smile for the exam. They staggered. Kael's hand found their elbow—scar-side out, honest heat. "Stay with the dirt," Kael said. "Look at your nails. Look at my ugly mark. Don't look at the polish." Nahl looked. Ridge grit. Scar-light. Mira's chalk-smeared cheek. Corvath's wing shadow falling crooked across stones that wanted to be a perfect grid and could not quite manage it while a dragon stood on them humming off-key. Aureon's shovel planted like a claim that claimed nothing. Orphiel's blank leaf trembling as if it wanted to catch the classroom and refuse to keep it. The classroom thinned. The children's faces became ordinary faces in the convoy—freckled, tired, unfinished. "Thank you," Nahl whispered. "Trace is hospitality," Kael said, embarrassed by how much he meant it. "That's all. I don't own your seeing. I just stay beside it." "Shared custody of the moment," Mira said dryly. "Put it on the map before you romanticize it."

Aureon walked the center of the convoy with the shovel, stopping sometimes to dig a small, useless hole and fill it again. People stared. A god wasting motion was a sermon without words. Command-hunger hated wasted motion. The memory-fields around him softened into ordinary wrongness—potholes, graffiti, a wall that leaned like a tired friend, a joke scrawled in charcoal: INDEXES CAN'T DANCE. "Why the holes?" a boy asked, hopping the edge of one. "So the road remembers it can be unfinished," Aureon said. "And so I remember I am not a finished answer. If I stop digging nonsense, I start digging thrones." The boy considered this with the seriousness of the young. "Can I dig one?" "Please," Aureon said, and handed over the shovel as if handing over a crown that had finally found honest work.

Veylan waited at a fork where a polished sign offered Direct Civic Welcome in letters so even they seemed to hum. His path had been faster; he looked rested in a way that made Nahl's stomach tighten. Behind him, two Index greeters held clipboards like shields made of manners. "The direct path is safe," Veylan said. "I have verified the greeters. No one will be harmed. You can end this theater and arrive as citizens instead of a parable." "Harm is not only bruises," Corvath said. "Sometimes harm is becoming easy to file. I was easy to file once. I filed others. The drawers still talk to me when the wind is wrong." Veylan's gaze flicked to Nahl's Seal-shape under cloth. "And sometimes stubbornness is vanity wearing a martyr's coat. The Lid is not a monster under a bed, Bearer. It is a solution for a world that cannot stop bleeding stories into every street."

Nahl did not step back. Doorstop. Feet planted. "In my homeland," they said carefully, "vanity was finishing other people's sentences. Solutions were sweet. The Lid tasted like mercy until no one remembered how to cry without filing a form. I am learning to leave blanks. Blanks are not wounds you failed to close. Blanks are rooms." For a moment Veylan's face opened—curiosity, almost respect, the shadow of a man who might once have loved living pages—and then the Perfectscribe closed again into patience. "Then follow your gold weather. I will walk where I can still be of use. Use is not a crime." "Use becomes a crime," Orphiel said softly, "when it erases the used." Veylan inclined his head as if accepting a footnote, not a rebuke, and took the direct path alone for a stretch—a white figure on clean stone. The convoy kinked left into a fish-seller's approach that stank of salt, scale, and honesty. Mira grinned without joy. "He will meet us inside. Indexes love reunions. They feel like order." "Then we reunite unfinished," Orphiel said, and wrote nothing, which was his bravest habit.

Kael Trace-marked the fork with two incomplete glyphs that only made sense as a pair. Alone, each looked like a slip of the hand. Together they said, to anyone who still read scar-script: We chose the stink on purpose. The fish-seller's approach taught the feet before it taught the mind. Gutters ran. Scales glittered like discarded coins. A woman with bare arms slapped a knife through silver bodies and sang the prices wrong on purpose when a clipboard approached, so the numbers would not settle into law. Children from the convoy pinched their noses, then forgot to pinch when a cat fight broke out over a head and became more interesting than stink. "My mother would faint," Nahl said, almost fond. "My mother would buy the cheap catch and make a miracle," Kael said. "Then complain the miracle had bones. Bones are how you know it was a fish and not a form." Sancora bought three skewers and made the greediest children wait their turn, which was also medicine. Harmonix tapped a crate in a rhythm that refused march-time; a dock worker joined without asking what the song meant. Meaning, the dock had decided, was optional if the beat kept you human. Orphiel paused where memory-stone met ordinary mud and pressed the Listening Leaf to a piling. The page fluttered, caught a smear of river-old truth, and left it unwritten. "The city remembers being a port before it remembered being a file," he said. "We should encourage that nostalgia." Corvath's wings twitched as a grid of birds tried once more overhead. Harmonix did not even look up; she clapped once, late, and the grid became a quarrel of wings. Feathers drifted into the fish gutter and became part of the lane's autobiography.

"Passport still good?" Aureon asked Nahl, nodding at their hands. Nahl showed him the nails. Ridge. Furrow. Fish-lane grit now, salt and scale. "If clean hands are the only ticket, I am permanently abroad." "Good," Aureon said. "Abroad is where neighbors are made." They climbed the last slant toward the under-lip. Behind them the polished Direct Civic Welcome shone like a tooth. Ahead, the city's breath came warm and argumentative, full of yeast and wet stone and the ozone of lattice under stress. Mira rolled the Wound-Chart so the gold kink led and the red filaments trailed like bad advice no one was obliged to take. "Last chance to pretend we are tourists," she said. "We were never tourists," Corvath answered. "Tourists do not arrive with dirt as paperwork." Nahl touched the Seal through cloth—not to wake it, only to admit it was there, guest and burden and wet animal. The hum that answered was neither fear nor triumph. It was readiness the way a threshold is ready: not eager, not closed, simply true.

They entered the city's under-lip at midmorning. Thresholds opened like mouths learning to speak without finishing every sentence. No doors. Many lintels. Curtains hung in temple mouths that had once, in the first Dawns, been torn free of hinges and never replaced; some curtains were already being sold as "soft privacy solutions" by smiling vendors with too-clean carts. The air smelled of bread, wet stone, ink, and the faint ozone of living lattice under stress. A woman sat on a step mending a net and singing a name that did not resolve. A man argued with a lamppost that had begun to glow in Index-white; he won by draping it in a child's painted shirt until the light looked ridiculous and therefore free. Somewhere a choir practiced Scar-Interval and failed beautifully, holding two tones until a dog howled and everyone laughed as if laughter were a third tone the Index could not catalog. Nahl's Seal hummed—not alarm, not triumph. Recognition. A city that had practiced open temples was a city that might understand a doorstop. Still, the pressure of the Lid—distant, white, patient—pressed behind the temples like a headache wearing perfume. "Feels like the village," Kael said, rewrapping his scar where the linen had slipped. "Louder. Meaner. Same refusal." "Same hospitality exam," Mira said, marking the map with a crooked star. "Pass or fail by whether we leave people more finished than we found them." "Fail on purpose, then," Corvath rumbled. "I have been finished. It did not suit me. Finishing felt like flying with clipped wings that still cast pretty shadows."

Aureon set the shovel's blade gently against the first public stone and left a smudge of ridge clay there like a signature no Index could notarize without dirt in its mouth. The boy who had dug the nonsense hole pressed his own thumbprint beside the god's smudge and looked fiercely proud. "Welcome," said a child from a balcony, not to them specifically, to the morning. "Don't close anything you can't open again." Sancora touched Nahl's shoulder—brief, professional, kind. "If the fields return in your sleep, wake someone. Ugly visions hate company." "I will," Nahl said, and meant it, which was new. In the finished homeland, waking someone was an imposition. Here it might be Trace. Harmonix tossed a last off-beat clap into the street. A flock of ordinary pigeons erupted from a ledge and refused to form a grid. Gold weather thickened over the open courts like a blessing that refused to be a decree. Nahl looked at their nails one last time before the crowd took them. Dirt still under. Passport still valid. The Seal's hum braided with the city's unfinished sentences until, for a few steps, they could not tell which was guest and which was host. They walked in. At the last checkpoint before the memory-fields, a greeter offered Kael a warm cloth for his hands. "Cleanliness is courtesy," she said. Kael thanked her and wiped only his left hand. The right, scarred, he left dirty on purpose. The greeter's smile flickered—software of kindness hitting a case it had not been trained for—and she waved him into the longer gold queue where questions were still allowed. Nahl, watching, copied the gesture with solemn mischief. Mira laughed once, sharp and grateful. "That's cartography," she said. "Leaving a mark the map can't sand off."

chapters.part: Act III — The Road of Living Scars
chapters.label: Chapter 18
chapters.title: City of Open Temples
paragraphs: After departure with dirt still under their nails, the road gave them a city that had built its hospitality out of ruins nobody had agreed to mourn. The city had torn its temple doors off in the Dawns and kept the thresholds as hospitality exams. From the under-lip the convoy spilled into streets that remembered how to argue. Vendors called prices that changed mid-sentence if the buyer looked too finished. A flock of pigeons refused a grid without needing Harmonix, as if the city itself had learned the clap. Kael's scar cooled in the ordinary mess and itched only when a white sash passed too near. You stepped under a lintel and the lintel asked—without words, with air and light and the particular quiet of a room that refused to own you—whether you came to kneel, to seize, or to sit. Most people sat. Sitting had become a kind of theology. Benches were scarred with initials and arguments. Floors kept the scuffs of dances that never resolved into processions. Where doors had hung, empty hinges remained like honest scars; children hung ribbons from them and called the ribbons temporary, which was the only kind of forever the city trusted.

Now Index soft-power offered curtains. Not doors, the vendors insisted. Never doors. Soft privacy. Thermal kindness. A way to keep night air from troubling the devout. The cloth was white enough to hum. When drawn, it did not lock—locking would have been honest tyranny—but it closed the exam. Thresholds became rooms again. Rooms became files. Aureon found a temple mouth on the second street where three such curtains hung like polite lies. He took one down with both hands, folded it with a farmer's care, and wrapped it around the shoulders of a woman whose teeth were chattering from more than cold. "Function over symbolism," he said when a greeter protested. "Blankets are harder to file as heresy. If your cloth warms, it serves. If it only hides, it serves someone else." The greeter's smile held. "Lightfather, privacy is not a Lid." "Privacy that erases the open is practicing," Aureon said. "I have seen practice become law while good people slept." He pulled the second curtain down. Corvath took the third, sniffed it, made a face, and tore a strip to bandage a child's scraped knee. The remaining cloth became a picnic groundcover by noon, stained with soup and therefore liberated. Nahl watched from a step, Seal quiet against their sternum. "In my city," they said to Kael, "we called curtains mercy. Mercy meant you did not have to see the unfinished faces in the street." "Here unfinished faces are the street," Kael said. He Trace-marked the empty hinges with incomplete hooks—places for ribbons, questions, hands. "If someone hangs a curtain again, the mark will itch. That's the idea, anyway." "Your scar has opinions about fabric now?" "My scar has opinions about anything that pretends to be kindness while measuring the door."

Missing memories showed as polite gaps. A baker could not recall her dead brother's laugh—only that grief had been "resolved" last spring by a visiting counselor with clean hands. A boy knew he had a grandmother and could not remember whether she liked salt or sugar on porridge; the question made him smile too calmly. In the plaza of three fountains, people moved through their days with the serenity of sanded wood. Sancora hated serenity that did not cost anything. She and those who still remembered silence-songs raised story-tents: canvas patched, poles crooked, interiors smelling of tea and wet wool. No stage. No single speaker. A circle of mats and a rule written in charcoal on a board that leaned: Tell the ugly true thing. Stop when you need. Do not fix the teller into a moral.

The first night was loud. A man sobbed the name of a daughter the Index had edited into "a completed chapter." A woman described a war wound that healed too clean and left her unable to trust weather. Nahl sat at the tent's edge and did not speak until a girl asked if foreign Seals ate memories. "No," Nahl said. Their voice shook and did not hide it. "Finished systems eat memories and call the meal peace. My Seal hums when you leave a place empty on purpose. Like a chair. Like a pause in a song." "Can I hum too?" the girl asked. "Please," Nahl said. "Badly." She hummed off-key. Harmonix, passing with a kettle, added a second tone that refused resolution. Scar-Interval leaked into the plaza. Gold weather thickened until even the Index lamps looked slightly embarrassed by their own evenness. Some nights after that were louder still. Loudness was gold weather. Finish faction pamphlets appeared under tent flaps—Noise Is Not Healing—and were used to start cookfires. The ash went into Sancora's pouch labeled, without irony, Future tomatoes.

Continuance circles formed without a name yet. Neighbors met in courtyards and under unfinished arches to witness without owning: a dispute about water rights held open until both parties admitted fear; a marriage argument paused by children playing doorstop across the threshold; a scribe's confession that he had almost sold his second name for a clean ledger. Trace-marks were shared—Kael taught three street-scribes how to leave doors ajar in their letters, how an unfinished curve could keep a sentence from becoming a verdict. "If you close the letter," Kael told them, chalk on his lip, "you close the person. Leave a hook. Leave a breath. If your master hates it, blame my scar. Scars are hard to demote." Mira updated maps with admitted ignorance. Here be wrongness we have not yet earned the right to correct. Host faction made the watermark a joke-prayer. Finish faction called it vandalism of certainty.

Veylan attended a Continuance circle once. He sat correctly. He listened with professional stillness. He took notes in a hand so neat it made Orphiel's shoulders climb toward his ears. When a woman described losing the smell of her husband's shirts, Veylan wrote for a long time. Then he left early, bowing to no one in particular. A child—freckled, sticky with fruit—stole the notes from the bench where Veylan had set them "for a moment" and ran, laughing, to Mira as if delivering treasure. Mira read. Her mouth went flat. "Closure recommendations," she said. "Formatted already. Suggest temporary containment of Unwritten Seal for children's sleep. Suggest story-tent volume limits. Suggest curtain grants for open temples. Suggest reclassification of Scar-Interval as public disturbance. He didn't even wait to hate us honestly. He filed us while we were still speaking." Corvath took the page, sniffed it, and handed it to Orphiel. "Burn or mud?" "Mud," Orphiel said. "Burn makes slogans. Mud makes compost." He pressed the neat page into a planter of city dirt until the ink ran into roots. "Let something living eat the recommendations."

Nahl stood three paces from the planter, doorstop to an impulse they did not name—whether to chase Veylan or to hide. "He believes he is kind." "The worst Indexes do," Corvath said. "I did. Kindness without room is a polished drawer." Aureon slept that night in a public square on a mat that smelled of horse and rain. He could have had any guest loft. He chose the square because squares were where thrones used to grow, and he wanted his body to remember stone without elevation. People stepped around him. A few sat nearby and talked about bean prices as if a god were furniture, which was the highest praise he could imagine. Toward middle-night, someone left him a crown of bread—rolls braided into a circle, still warm, a child's idea of glory. Aureon woke to the smell, sat up, and laughed once, quiet as ash settling. He ate the crown with soup a night vendor insisted was "only onions and luck." Corvath found him there at the edge of dawn, crumbs on a god's chin, shovel under one hand like a scepter that had finally relaxed. "Best use of a crown I have seen," Corvath said. "It was never meant for heads," Aureon answered. "Heads get ideas. Stomachs get honesty." He offered Corvath a heel of the bread-crown. Corvath took it. They chewed in companionable silence while the square woke into arguments and pigeons and a woman sweeping steps with more force than dust required.

Across the square, Nahl sat doorstop at a debate that had almost become a vote. The motion, framed politely: Box the Seal for the children's sleep. Temporary. Compassionate. Reversible under committee review. Finish voices spoke of nightmares, of foreign glyphs, of the Lid's distant white promise that no child would ever again wake screaming unfinished names. Host voices spoke of hospitality exams, of curtains-as-doors, of the day doors returned and no one noticed until kneeling felt natural again. Nahl did not give a speech. They sat on the bottom step of the open temple where the debate spilled, body across the rush of people trying to reach the front with petitions already formatted. When a man tried to step over them, Nahl looked up and said, mild as mint tea, "I am a doorstop. Walk around or sit. Do not finish me into a corridor." The man sat. Then another. The vote dissolved into conversation. Conversation dissolved into shared bread. The motion remained unfinished on the board, charcoal trailing off mid-word like a thought that had chosen life over closure. Which was victory.

Kael, watching from the side with the street-scribes, felt his scar cool. Mira marked the square on her map with a gold kink and the note: Debate ended without ending. Keep. Orphiel wrote on the Listening Leaf, crooked and glad: Doorstop is culture now. Index translation failed. Veylan, at the plaza's far edge, watched the unfinished motion and did not smile. For the first time since the ridge, he looked less patient than tired—as if patience itself had begun to cost him something he could not file.

On the second evening, Kael and Nahl walked a circuit of open temple mouths to count curtains. They found eleven new ones since morning. They took down four that were empty theater—no cold bodies, only the wish to close—and left seven that truly warmed sleepers, after Aureon's test: if the cloth could become a blanket without anyone mourning the threshold, it could stay until dawn and then be folded into the common pile. A greeter tried to cite provisional code. Nahl stood doorstop on the citation's path until the greeter, sighing, walked around. "You enjoy that," Kael said. "I enjoy not being a key," Nahl corrected. "The standing is only anatomy." They bought fried dough from a cart whose owner refused Index tokens and took only stories or coin that had dirt on it. Nahl paid with a half-memory spoken soft: the museum case, the hum, the run. The owner wiped his eyes with a floury hand and gave them extra salt. "For the road back into yourself," he said.

At a Continuance circle in a laundry courtyard, wet sheets hung like honest ghosts. People confessed small finishes they regretted—a joke sanded of its edge, a child's question answered too completely, a letter sealed that should have stayed ajar. Mira arrived late, chalk in her hair, and confessed forcing a road in her apprenticeship. The circle did not absolve her. It witnessed. Absolution was a kind of closure; witness was a kind of door. Veylan's stolen-and-mudded notes had become a quiet legend. Someone set a blank page on a bench with a sign: Leave your closure recommendations here for compost. By midnight the page held three neat paragraphs and a child's drawing of a dragon eating a clipboard. Orphiel collected the lot for Bloom's ash pile with ceremonial glee.

By the third day the city had begun to treat the convoy as weather rather than spectacle. That was better. Spectacles got finished into festivals and festivals got finished into schedules. Weather you argued with, dressed for, thanked, cursed, and shared. Kael taught Trace in a side alley to anyone who brought their own chalk; by evening the alley walls were full of incomplete hooks, and a baker used one as a place to hang her second-best ladle so she would remember not to inventory joy. Mira sold no maps and gave away three Wound-Chart scraps with watermarks already bleeding, instructing recipients to ruin them further. "If it stays pretty," she said, "you've failed the assignment." Nahl learned the names of two hinge-ribbons—children had named them Maybe and Not Yet—and sat under them during a rain that refused to be even. Water sheeted through open temple mouths and people cheered as if the rain were a guest who had finally stopped being polite. Sancora put out basins and called the collection unclean stock for later teas. Orphiel stood in the wet with the Listening Leaf inside his coat and looked as happy as a blank page allowed. Aureon helped a carpenter rehang nothing on a lintel—only sand the empty hinge so it would not rust closed in spirit. "Maintenance of absence," the carpenter said, trying the phrase. "Best liturgy I've heard today," Aureon said, and meant it more than any hymn that resolved on time.

Corvath found a basement where Finish and Host played cards badly together, bets paid in stories instead of coin. He did not join the game. He sat on the stairs and let his shadow be a blanket when the lamp flickered Index-white, and when the lamp steadied into ordinary flame someone dealt him in without asking his allegiance. He lost three rounds and paid with a true story about drawers. The table went quiet, then loud, then human again. Veylan was seen at the edge of two more circles and left early both times without notes anyone could steal. The child-thief network reported disappointment. Mira reported caution. Nahl reported, only to Kael, a strange pity that did not forgive. "Pity can be a Lid too," Kael said. "I know," Nahl said. "I am leaving it unfinished. Neither weapon nor absolution."

Night came again with story-tents and off-beat clapping and curtains folded into blankets for anyone cold. The city of open temples breathed through its empty hinges. Someone had chalked on a plaza stone: SIT FIRST. Someone else had added: THEN ARGUE. A third hand, smaller, had drawn a doorstop wearing a crown of bread crumbs. Far off, something white and smooth waited like a period at the end of a sentence no one had agreed to finish. Closer, yeast and rain and tomato-ash dreams rose from kitchens that had not accepted any schedule of silence. Before sleep fully took the square, Kael sat with three street-scribes and practiced leaving letters half-open on scrap, then sending the scraps to no one—burning them instead, ash for Bloom. "The point isn't delivery," he said. "The point is teaching your hand not to close by reflex." One scribe cried without explaining. Sancora, passing with tea, did not ask. Unexplained tears were allowed to remain unfinished data. Nahl slept on a borrowed mat near Aureon's square and dreamed not of classrooms but of tables with empty places kept empty on purpose—and of bread crowns eaten down to crumbs that birds argued over without forming a grid. In the dream Serenya's kind of quiet sat at the empty place without filling it, and Nahl, for once, did not flinch from a silence that was a room. A street preacher tried to crown Aureon with words. Aureon bought the man's soup and asked about the recipe until the sermon died of nutrition. Continuance strangers later called it the Soup Doctrine. Aureon called it lunch. In the city a curtain salesman rebranded closures as privacy; Continuance strangers bought the cloth and cut rain-capes with uneven hems. The salesman complained to no one who would neat the complaint.
The curtain trade took them four days to understand, and Mira took it personally.

On the surface it was nothing: a stall near the eastern arch sold cloth. Heavy, grey, lined, expensive, advertised with a painted hand drawing a curtain closed and a caption that read *Soft Privacy. Not a Door. Never a Door.* The vendor's name was Amel, he had a fine honest face and a bad cough, and he explained—patiently, repeatedly, to anyone who would listen—that the Index produced nothing in this city, only stocked: the cloth was woven by the mill cooperative, the lining by a widow's guild, the brass rings by a family that had made brass rings for six generations. All of it was local. All of it was fair. All of it paid wages that Arrived On Time.

"That is the horrible part," Mira said, on the second day, having interviewed the wrecker, the widow, and the ring-family and found nothing rotten in any of them. "There is no villain in this stall. There is a *supply chain*. The Index stopped needing hands. It only needs order."

Kael found the boy two alleys over, which was the point at which the stall stopped being a mystery and became an injury. The boy was maybe eleven. He sat on a step with a broken toy cart in his hands and he could not remember whether he had had a brother. He knew, because his mother had told him, that he had had one, and that the brother had been older, and that the brother had died in the winter, and that the brother's name had been Innes. He could not remember the laugh. His mother could not remember it either. She had been offered, at a stall not unlike Amel's, a night's soft sleep in a curtained bed in a quiet room, at a price she could afford; and the next morning her grief had become orderly, and her son's name-list had lost a line, and the room had been so *nice*.
"Where is the room?" Kael asked.

"Folded away," the woman said, which turned out to be exactly literal. Mira found the address: a former shrine on the city's north side, deconsecrated and re-fitted with forty curtained alcoves. You went in with a grief and came out with a receipt. The alcoves were clean. The alcoves were cheap. The alcoves had a *satisfaction rate*, posted by the door in a decent hand, ninety-four percent.

Kael told the woman he could not get the laugh back, which was true and which he said at once because Orphiel had taught him that hope sold too early is a kind of theft. What he could do was worse and better than a laugh: he could sit with her and the boy and ask every question he had, and write down every fragment either of them produced, and put the fragments side by side on the step, and not tidy them. They did that for two hours. What they got was not a laugh. It was a list: a laugh that came out of the nose before the mouth; a laugh that had startled a cat; a laugh that had once got the brother thrown out of a temple for rudeness; a way he had of saying *Inga* when he meant *Innes* when he was tired. The boy added one line himself, near the end, in a hand that wandered: *he said my name like it had a door in it.*

The mother cried, which the alcove had promised she would not have to do. The boy wrote another line. Then Kael Trace-marked the scrap of paper incomplete and folded it and gave it to them and told them plainly that it was not their brother and it never would be and it was theirs to update for the rest of their lives, which was the exact sentence that made the woman laugh—a wet, startled, entirely unlovely laugh that came out of her mouth first and her nose second and made the cat knock a pot off the step.
"That's it," the boy said, with the flat certainty of an eleven-year-old delivering a verdict. "That was the laugh."

It probably was not. It was a laugh in the same family, on the same street, going in the same direction, and the boy would spend forty years deciding which parts were real and which parts were the day three strangers sat on his step refusing to be certain. That was the trade. The Index had offered one clean false comfort, free of charge, correctly filed. Kael and Mira and a broken toy cart offered one crooked true fragment with a lifetime of maintenance attached.

They told Amel the curtain vendor about it—not to shame him, which Mira insisted on, though she wanted to—and Amel stood in his honest stall with his honest cough and looked at the list, and then he did something nobody expected: he rolled up the week's unsold stock, carried it to the arch, and cut it, unevenly, into rain-capes and window shades and one spectacular bad hat, and gave them to the first fifteen people who walked past, which cost him the week's wages and gained him nothing at all. Mira logged the whole thing on the Wound-Chart under *supply chain, one link, human again*.

"Records," Orphiel said, watching Amel cut cloth, "are what you do when you do not trust the memory of a thing to survive. The Index has better records than any of us. That is the only advantage it has ever had."
"Then we write the crooked ones," Kael said.
"We write the *updatable* ones," Orphiel said, and went to fetch his pen.

That night, before any vote or vigilance list, the inner circle sat on Aureon's mat and played a foolish game Mira invented: each person named one true thing they had done badly that day without turning it into a lesson. Kael admitted he had Trace-marked a soup bowl. Nahl admitted they had flinched from a child's flower. Mira admitted she had yelled at a mile that did not deserve it. Corvath admitted he had enjoyed looking frightening for half a breath. Aureon admitted he had wanted, for one pure instant, to straighten a leaning shutter "just to help." Orphiel admitted he had almost neatened a margin. They laughed until a passerby asked if they were drunk. "On unfinishedness," Mira said. "Very cheap. Highly recommended." The passerby sat down and confessed he had nearly signed a curtain petition. No one filed him. Someone passed him bread-crown crumbs, and for a little while the city of open temples was only elbows, salt, and ordinary company—the kind of company Indexes never learn to inventory.

chapters.part: Act III — The Road of Living Scars
chapters.label: Chapter 19
chapters.title: The Market of Borrowed Glyphs
paragraphs: After the city of open temples let them sleep in its oldest argument, they went looking for a market where the dangerous goods were stacked in plain sight. The night market sold glyphs the way other markets sold spices—some honest borrowings, some poison, all of it fragrant enough to confuse the nose of conscience. They entered after dusk from a Continuance-friendly court where story-tents still hummed, following Mira's gold kink past three helpful guides whose smiles synchronized until Harmonix coughed off-beat and two of the smiles became ordinary greed. "Better," Mira said. "Greed I can map. Synchrony is fog."

Lamps hung at uneven heights. Smoke braided with fried dough, river fish, ink, and the sharp green smell of crushed herbs used to wake Trace when Trace grew sleepy. Stalls leaned into one another like gossiping neighbors. Children ran with ribbons that had once been Index curtains and were now simply cloth with a past. Above the alleys, the open temples kept their empty hinges; above the temples, far and pale, the Lid-district's unfinished tower watched like a pupil dilated by patience.

Mira charted stalls by weather color before she let anyone spend a coin. Gold stalls taught practices: how to mend a net without cursing the tear into shame; how to remember a dead name by cooking the dish they burned; how to leave a question open at the end of a letter so the receiver remained a person instead of a conclusion. The gold felt warm on Mira's Wound-Chart. Ink ran toward those tables like a dog toward a familiar door. Red stalls sold finished seals that branded the buyer calm and empty. Little metal discs. Soft white threads. A paste you rubbed on the tongue to "resolve anxiety into clarity." People left those tables smiling with the serenity of sanded wood. Kael's scar screamed near red—bright, precise, a warning that did not bother with manners.

He learned to trust the scream. "If my hand panics," he told Nahl, flexing under linen, "we do not debate. We leave. Philosophy can catch up when we are not being edited." "In my homeland the scream would be called resistance to wellness," Nahl said. They kept three paces from a red stall whose vendor wore Veylan's kind of patience like perfume. "I am trying to prefer pain that tells the truth." Orphiel drifted with the Listening Leaf half-open, buying nothing until a gold-stall woman offered him a blank scrap and said, "For the things you are brave enough not to write." He bowed as if she had knighted him with absence.

Mid-market, under a canopy of patched sails, a stall offered Lid fragments. They lay on black cloth like pieces of a sky that had decided to become metal. Smooth. Kind to the eye. When a loud argument broke out two stalls over—two fishmongers disputing the soul of a mackerel—the nearest fragment brightened and the argument dropped to a murmur, then to smiles, then to a handshake that satisfied neither face. Nahl nearly vomited. They caught the edge of Mira's sleeve, breath gone thin. "That is my homeland's skin," they whispered. "That quiet. That kindness that ends the need to speak. Do not touch it. Do not let it touch you." Kael's scar wrote a jagged scrap of light across his palm: KEY-METAL. RADIUS. FEAR-FAT. He showed Nahl without speaking. Nahl nodded, eyes wet, jaw set.

The vendor smiled. "Peace radius, friends. Ten feet of civic calm. Ideal for schools, debates, and households with difficult memories. No chains. No doors. Only quiet." "Quiet is a tool," Corvath said, stepping in so his wing-shadow fell across the fragments. "I used quieter tools than this to end names. How much for one—if the price includes your honesty about where the metal learned its manners?" The vendor's smile did not slip. "Salvage from eastern vault-works. Pre-Dawn adjacent. Perfectly legal under provisional Index hospitality codes." "Legal," Corvath repeated, tasting the word like spoiled milk. "Orphiel." Orphiel bought one fragment with full disclosure, counting coins slowly so the market could hear. "I am purchasing a danger to study," he announced to anyone listening, which was everyone within two stalls. "I will not wear it. I will not worship it. I will lock it in dirt." He did. On the spot. A mud box from Sancora's pack—rough, thumbprinted, labeled in charcoal: DO NOT WORSHIP. The fragment went in. Dirt went over. The quiet radius hiccuped and died like a lie caught mid-sentence. The fishmongers' argument resumed at full volume, glorious and stupid, and both of them looked more alive for it. "Study requires dirt," Orphiel said, sealing the box with twine. "Clean study is how Lids recruit scholars." Nahl stood doorstop between the stall and a cluster of curious children until the vendor, still smiling, lowered his canopy as if the night had simply grown colder.

A black-sun map appeared on a table with no seller. No canopy. No coins. Only a sheet of pale hide and ink the color of eclipses: the city drawn true enough to hurt, with a perfect circle where a tower would be—white, smooth, finished in the drawing though unfinished in stone. Around the circle, streets bent into obedience. Story-tents were absent. Open temple hinges were sketched as closed. In the corner, a neat legend: Projected Continuance under Complete Index. Mira's hands hovered. "If I copy it perfect, I feed it." "If you ignore it, you walk blind," Kael said. "Then I copy it incomplete." She set her charcoal to work. The circle she left broken—an open C, a mouth, a wound. She smeared the legend until Complete became a smudge that might have been Compost. She watermarked the margin in her cramped hand: This map is already wrong; update me. The copy stayed living. Lines shifted as the night market breathed. A gold kink appeared where the fish lane stank hardest. A Finish buyer at the next table paid for a perfect copy from a sudden clerk who might always have been there. The perfect copy went inert and cold in his hands, a dead fish of paper. He smiled calmly and said it was beautiful. Kael's scar agreed it was dead. "Pretty cages," Corvath murmured. "Same old song." Nahl stared at the broken circle on Mira's living sheet. "That tower wants me as key." "Then we visit it as people," Mira said, rolling the Wound-Chart so the broken circle stayed visible at the edge. "Not as hardware."

Too many helpful guides appeared after that. Young people with clean sashes offered to lead the convoy by the straightest alleys. Old people with gentle voices recommended avenues "recently improved for safety." Smiles synchronized when the party paused; for a heartbeat half the market grinned on the same beat, a choir of faces without Scar-Interval. Harmonix clapped off-beat once, hard. Several smiles faltered into real expressions—irritation, fear, ordinary greed. The market exhaled. "They're herding us," Mira said. "Red weather under gold paint." "Then take the road the Index aesthetics hate," Sancora suggested. "I can smell one." They smelled it before they saw it: fish-stench lane, guts and salt and the sweet rot of things that had been honest animals. No synchronized smiles there. Gutters ran with water that remembered being a river. A woman sang a work song with a cracked high note and did not apologize. Cats owned the corners. A man sold fried fins on sticks and argued politics with a gull. Mira routed the party through.

Veylan found them halfway down, ledger under his arm, nose wrinkled despite discipline. "This is unnecessary," he said. "You endanger children for the romance of filth." "Filth is a witness," Mira said. "Your straight alleys have too many friends." "Friends are not Index." "Friends who smile on the same beat are," Kael said, scar still hot from the red stalls. "Come or don't. The fish don't care about your ledger." Veylan came. Perhaps pride. Perhaps the first unfiled curiosity. He walked carefully, boots finding the least offensive stones, and said nothing for a long stretch while the lane taught him that the city had innards. Nahl laughed once—startled, sudden—when a cat dropped a fish head at their feet like an offering. The sound broke out of them raw. The Seal hummed gold as if laughter were a kind of Trace, as if joy without resolution were a practice the Unwritten recognized. Kael grinned. "Keep doing that. My scar likes it." "I am not a performance," Nahl said, still half-laughing, half-shaken. "No," Kael said. "You're a person in a stinking lane. That's better."

Orphiel hugged the mud box to his ribs. Inside, the Lid fragment pulsed once against the dirt—annoyed, or hungry, or lonely for quiet—and then subsided. Study, not worship. Mud, not altar. At the lane's far mouth the night market's noise returned in ordinary chaos. Gold weather held. Far above, the black-sun's perfect circle remained a threat drawn on living hide, broken in Mira's copy, waiting in the city's north like a period that believed itself inevitable. Near midnight a red stall tried to move—wheels under black cloth, smiling porters, a route that would have cut across the fish lane's mouth like a neat erasure. Mira saw the weather shift on her chart and barked a laugh that was all teeth. "They're trying to pave the stink with calm," she said. "Kael—scream check." Kael walked toward the moving stall until his scar lit the linen from within. "Confirmed. Harm in a box." Corvath and Aureon did not smash it. Smashing made martyrs of furniture. They simply sat on the lane's stones with a picnic of cold fish and bread crown crumbs and invited half the market to join, clogging the wheels with living bodies and ordinary hunger. The porters asked them to move for civic flow. Harmonix started a Scar-Interval work song. The stall's finished seals dimmed as if embarrassed by melody that would not resolve. Nahl stood doorstop at the stall's tongue—the opening where buyers entered—and said to each approaching face, mild as mint, "If you need quiet, sit with a friend. If you need emptiness, this metal will sell you a grave and call it a spa." Some turned away angry. Some turned away thoughtful. One Finish teenager bought nothing and asked Kael to teach them an incomplete mark instead. Kael did, right there, chalk on wet stone, while the red stall's wheels squeaked in defeated patience. Veylan watched from a balcony of clean brick and did not descend to help the porters. That non-descent was a kind of map update. Mira noted it without kindness or cruelty: Veylan withheld aid to red mobile—crack widens. When the stall finally retreated, the fish lane smelled like victory and guts. Orphiel patted the mud box. "You stayed buried. Good metal." The fragment pulsed once, sulking, and the dirt held.

On the way to sleep they stopped where a gold-stall elder taught the practice of borrowed glyphs done right. "Borrowing is not theft if you leave the source richer," she said, chalking a curve that looked like Kael's incompletes and was not. "You take a mend-sign from a fisher and you bring back a story of a net that held. You take a grief-mark from a widow and you bring back company, not a copy of her dead. Finished seals sold red across the way? Those are thefts that call themselves gifts. Your body will know. If it goes quiet too fast, run." Nahl practiced a borrow from the elder's grief-mark—only a finger-trace in air, not on skin—and felt the Seal answer with a warmth that asked permission of no museum. "I have stolen before," they said. "Then practice returning," the elder said. "Return is Trace's cousin." Kael left an ugly incomplete on her stall-leg as payment and thanks. She snorted. "That will scare the red-buyers. Perfect."

Mira bought nothing and stole nothing and still left richer, Wound-Chart updated with a note: Honest borrow stalls—gold; Lid skin—mud only; black-sun perfect copies—dead on arrival. She showed Veylan the note without softness. "Your aesthetics hate fish. Remember what saved us when you recommend avenues." Veylan's jaw worked. "I remember. Memory is not the same as agreement." "It never is," Mira said. "That's why we map both." Corvath carried the mud box for a stretch so Orphiel's arms could rest. Inside, the fragment pulsed once against dirt like a sulking heart. Corvath hummed off-key until it subsided. "I used to quiet rooms with fear," he told the box. "Now I quiet you with compost. Improve yourself." Aureon paid a street-child in bread crown crumbs from a pocket—somehow he still had crumbs—to watch for synchronized smiles and report them by off-beat clap. The child took the job with solemn glee and clapped the convoy home crooked through two more alleys the Index had not bothered to pretty. They slept that night in a loft above a net-mender's shop, fish smell in the rafters, doorstop games on the floorboards, and for a few hours the Index's helpful smiles could not find the rhythm of their breath. Nahl's last waking thought was the cat with the fish head, and the laugh that had escaped them, and the Seal's gold hum as if joy without resolution were a practice older than any Lid.

chapters.part: Act III — The Road of Living Scars
chapters.label: Chapter 20
chapters.title: Ambush of Perfect Lines
paragraphs: After the market of borrowed glyphs took nothing from them but time, the perfect lines came for them in an alley that had been measured twice. The avenue appeared overnight—perfect flagstones, perfect lamps, perfect width for orderly walking. Dawn found the convoy already tense; fish-lane sleep had been honest but short, and the mud box had pulsed twice in the night like a tooth. Mira woke with red filaments clawing her chart's margin and swore before her eyes fully opened. "It's here," she said. "Straightness. Fresh. Expensive." Yesterday the block had been a tangle of repair scaffolds, leaning walls, and a mural of the Dawns with muddy hands. Today the mural was gone, or edited into pure light so thoroughly that even memory of mud felt rude. The stones fit without a seam. The lamps glowed Index-white at intervals measured by someone who loved numbers more than eyes. Along both sides, flower boxes held identical blooms that did not smell of anything.

Mira stood at the mouth of it with her Wound-Chart open and swore in three dialects, one of them cartographic. "Red weather dressed as civic pride," she said. "Cul-de-sac behind us went redder at dawn—closed loop, no exit without smiling. This avenue is the only gold the map will admit, which means the map is being bribed." "Then we don't take it," Kael said. "Then we freeze in a red pocket until calm becomes our only verb," Mira answered. "We take it knowing it's a throat. We do not swallow. We kick on the way down." Nahl's Seal hummed a thin, anxious phrase. They looked at their nails—dirt still under from the fish lane, passport against polish—and nodded. "In my homeland avenues like this were called mercy corridors. They led to exams." "Here they lead to pavilions," Corvath said. He had smelled the old hunger under the flowers. "I know the architecture of helpful endings."

Veylan arrived with two greeters and a calm that tried to be contagious. "The renovation is for festival safety. You invent sieges in every straight line. Walk. I will walk with you. No harm." Aureon rested the shovel across his shoulders. "If there is harm, it will wear a smile. That is not reassurance." They entered because the alternative was a red-weather cul-de-sac where second names had already begun to thin at the edges of children's voices.

Midway, lines of force rose like chalk in air. They were beautiful the way diagrams are beautiful: clean, explanatory, certain. They herded without touching, a geometry of suggestion that became command if you believed suggestions were neutral. The avenue's perfect width narrowed into a funnel toward a white pavilion pitched so neatly it seemed less built than filed into place. Archivists waited with forms. Not soldiers. Never soldiers if they could help it. Men and women in soft gray with pens that never blotched and eyes that had practiced kindness until kindness became a technique. Behind them, a glove of white force hung in the air like a hand that did not need a body.

"Travelers," the lead Archivist said, voice warm as milk. "Provisional registration for the Unwritten anomaly and associated persons. Temporary containment language only. Children's sleep is our mutual concern. Sign, and the city continues open." Veylan called for calm. "Do not make a scene. Scenes become riots in the record. Calm is how we keep agency." Calm was the weapon. Nahl felt it slide under the ribs—sweet, reasonable, a Lid-fragment's cousin. Around them, convoy members' shoulders dropped. A woman began to smile the sanded smile. A boy reached for a pen as if reaching for bread.

"Scar-Interval!" Harmonix snapped, and sang two tones that refused to resolve. The smile cracked. The boy blinked. Gold weather flared ugly and alive. Kael, Mira, and Orphiel threw a witness rope. They had braided it that morning without naming why: scar-thread from Kael's linen, map-twine from Mira's kit, blank-leaf strips Orphiel tore with apologies to the Listening Leaf. The braid was crooked. It hung wrong. It was the most beautiful wrong thing on the avenue. They cast it across the chalk lines. Where the rope hung crooked, the grid failed—force stuttering into visible seams, geometry sulking like a spoiled clerk. People scrambled through the mess. Children, understanding games better than treaties, smeared fruit from their pockets onto the perfect stones until sticky geometry lost its pride. A girl wrote OPE in apricot pulp and left the last letter for later.

"Forms are optional!" Orphiel shouted, which was not a legal argument and worked better than one. He held up the Listening Leaf, blank and trembling. "This page refuses your sentence. So do we." Clash without a king: no duel of champions, only many hands refusing the pavilion. Host faction shoved tables askew. Finish faction members hesitated—some helped the Archivists from fear, some discovered they hated white gloves more than foreign Seals and yanked pens out of soft gray hands. Aureon did not shine. He dug the shovel into a perfect flagstone and cracked it, a single honest wound in the avenue's face. "Lightfather—" an Archivist began. "Neighbor," Aureon corrected, and cracked another stone. "I am not your header."

The white glove moved for Nahl. It did not strike. It fitted—air shaping toward their chest, toward the Seal, toward the old grammar of key. Nahl tried to step back and found the chalk lines still half-alive around their ankles, polite as manacles. Corvath stepped between. He could have opened his wings into weapons of rule. He had done versions of that in older centuries. Instead he held them close and took the glove on his forearm, flesh and shadow-scale accepting burn rather than translating burn into domination. The smell was ozone and old libraries. His face went tight. He did not close the pain into a throne. "Between," he growled. "Not above. You do not get my old self as a gift." The glove flared, seeking a hierarchy to complete. Corvath gave it a scar instead—an unfinished refusal. Kael's Trace-marks sparked along the witness rope; Mira's broken black-sun circle on the Wound-Chart bled gold; Nahl, shaking, planted themselves as doorstop against the funnel's mouth so no child could be herded past into the pavilion's calm. "I will not be a key," Nahl said, voice raw enough to scrape the white air. "I will be a doorstop." The phrase, already culture, became weapon without becoming slogan. Convoy voices picked it up crooked. Doorstop. Doorstop. The pavilion's forms fluttered as if embarrassed.

Veylan stood in the chaos with his ledger open and for a heartbeat did not write. His eyes found Corvath's burning arm, Nahl's planted feet, the fruit-smeared stones. Something unfiled moved in his face. Then an Archivist thrust a pen at him and he took it by habit—and did not sign. The pen hung. The habit broke mid-gesture. "Move!" Mira yelled. "Cracks between buildings—Index renovations unfinished on the east side—go!" They escaped into those cracks: crooked passages where scaffolding still leaned, where murals still had muddy hands, where the living city had not yet been polished into a corridor. Gold weather poured through like apology from stone that remembered being free. Behind them the perfect avenue tried to reseal and could not quite, not with fruit and cracked flags and a witness rope still twitching across its pride.

Casualties: bruises; one lost second name recovered by Sancora's song until the woman wept and said again, uglier; Corvath's forearm blistered white at the edges; Kael's scar raw from over-Trace; Nahl's voice scraped thin; a certainty, shared and cold, that the Lid was near and hungry. In a narrow yard that smelled of cats and soap, Kael rewrapped his scar. Nahl wiped fruit from their cloak with hands that still shook. Mira sat on an overturned bucket, chalk-smeared, grinning like a cartographer who had survived a lie. "In my homeland this would be cataloged as riot," Nahl said. "Here we call it cartography," Mira answered. "The avenue was a false line. We mapped the refusal." Corvath accepted Sancora's unclean poultice without flinching. "Between hurts," he said. "Good. If it stopped hurting I would worry I had started ruling again." Aureon leaned on the shovel, cracked flagstone grit still on the blade. "No sieges," he said, more to himself than to them. "No crowns. We visit what hunts us. We do not become a pavilion with better intentions."

Veylan stood at the yard's edge, ledger closed. He had followed into the cracks. His boots were dirty for the first time in days. "You could have signed and slept," he said quietly. "We could have," Orphiel said, cradling the mud box where the Lid fragment pulsed like an angry heart. "Sleep is not the only mercy." Nahl looked north, where white pressure gathered beyond roofs. Doorstop instinct set their feet even in rest. The Seal hummed gold-thin, not safe, not finished—alive.

They did not celebrate. Celebration could become a parade, and parades loved avenues. Instead they passed water, counted heads, rewrapped linen, and let children cry without scheduling the tears. A Host woman and a Finish man argued about whether fruit on stones was vandalism or sacrament until both were laughing too hard to hold the argument closed. Sancora called that a clean wound. Nahl sat with their back to a wall that still had muddy hands in its mural and shook until the shaking became ordinary cold. Kael sat near without crowding. "You said the vow in a throat made of chalk," he said. "It held." "It held because many hands held it," Nahl said. "I am trying to remember plurality when the glove wants a single key." Orphiel pressed the Listening Leaf to Corvath's burn—not to record, to cool. The blank page warmed and left no ink, only a little less fire. "Witness without owning," Orphiel murmured. "Even pain."

Aureon walked the crack network with the shovel, tapping stones that rang too pure and cracking those until they sounded like a city again. "If perfection returns by morning, we repeat," he told a street-scribe. "Repetition without ritual is maintenance. Ritual without dirt is Index." In the hour after, they inventoried more than bruises. A Finish man who had helped the Archivists sat with his head in his hands while Sancora cleaned a scrape on his knuckle. "I thought calm was neutral," he said. "Calm is a tool," Sancora said. "Tools take sides when the hand that holds them has already chosen a drawer." He nodded, miserable and awake. Nahl brought him water and did not require an apology for the faction signs he had carried yesterday. "Be unfinishable," Nahl offered, awkward with the greeting still new in their mouth. "Working on it," the man said, and almost laughed.
The crack census started as spite and became a public service by the fourth hour, which Mira maintained all season was the normal career of spite.

She did it with chalk on a board in the market square, in her ugliest script, under a heading she refused to improve: THINGS IN THIS CITY THAT ARE NOT FINISHED, AND THE TWO KINDS OF ALMOST. Beneath it, two columns. In the left column she wrote *honest*: the alleys where the paving had sunk because carts had used it for two hundred years; the step by the fountain worn into a saddle by feet; the lintel on Fenwick Street that had been repaired badly in a war by a man who had signed his work in the iron. In the right column she wrote *bait*: the alley whose cracks had been scrubbed and filled overnight with a filler so smooth that children slid on it; the doorway where the seam had been painted to look old by a hand that had never in its life left a brushstroke crooked; the whole eastern terrace, whose roofs had been resolved into a single plane, which is not a thing roofs do.

By noon there were forty people at the board arguing, and by the second hour of the argument the beautiful and fatal thing happened: the city began to bring her its own cases. A baker who could not work out why his oven had stopped drawing. A woman whose wall had grown a straight line. Two brothers who had between them a courtyard that one of them had had repaired and the other could no longer stand to sit in. None of them had been paid. None of them had signed anything. They had merely, at various points in the last year, been *offered a service*, and it had been free, and it had been good, and their courtyards had become places they did not want to be.

"Here is the rule," Mira said, chalk up, to a square that was now two hundred people deep and entirely quiet, which is the kind of quiet that costs a person their voice if they misuse it. "A crack is bait if closing it made the place *quieter*. A crack is honest if leaving it has made somebody argue. That is the whole test. It is not perfect. It is not even good cartography. Use it and bring me your errors."

Kael stood at the board's edge with his slate and did the other half of the work, which was harder and less showy. He taught the four people who could not read. He found them one at a time and explained the two columns out loud, twice, and then had each of them tell *him* a case from their own street, and wrote it in the correct column while they watched, and then showed them which column their case had gone in and asked whether they agreed. Two of them corrected him. He changed both, in public, and the changing of them did more for the census than the census did.

Near dusk a Finish family came to the board with their sleeves already rolled, ready to be humiliated. They had been the eastern terrace. The father had accepted the roof work in the spring; the offer had come from a man with excellent manners and no forms, and it had been free, and the family had been so relieved to have the leak gone that they had stood in the courtyard together on the first rainy night and watched the water run off in a single straight sheet into the gutter, which the father now described, dry-eyed and precise, as the last happy evening they had in that house.
The square waited to see what Mira would do with them, because the square had a taste for verdicts and had learned enough that season to be ashamed of the taste and to want the verdict anyway.
Mira handed the father the chalk.

"Your terrace," she said. "Draw it wrong. Draw it the way it was, with the bad flashing and the crooked gable, and mark where the water used to come in, and be as inexact as you need. We are not fixing it. We are *un-resolving* it—which is a word I have just invented and will be telling Orphiel about at the earliest opportunity—and then your children will grow up in a house with a roof that has a history."

The father drew for twenty minutes. It was bad. His sons corrected him twice and he accepted both corrections, and by the end of it there were four people drawing on the board at once and a small crowd calling out details from the terrace's own memory, and the drawing became something no architect would have permitted, and the eldest son stood back from it and said, in the tone of a person discovering a fact, "It's ours again."

The census ran for six weeks. It listed three hundred and eleven things in the city that were not finished, and sixty-two things that were bait, and at the end of it Mira had a chart of the city such as had never existed—not because she had measured anything, but because two hundred people had argued in front of her about what their own streets meant, and she had written down the argument. Orphiel wanted it for the Codex. She refused, on the grounds that the Codex was a book and this was a *map*, and that if you bound it, the arguing would stop.
Veylan came to the board on the last day. He read both columns for a long time. Then he asked, mildly, whether a person could be listed.
"No," Mira said.
"A building, then. A city. A method of working."
"That thing in your satchel," Mira said, not looking up. "The one you haven't opened since the river."

Veylan did not answer. He went away and walked the eastern terrace, and stood in the courtyard of the family who had been so relieved, and looked up at the roof that had a history now, and took out his notebook, and wrote nothing in it, and put it away, and was seen by three witnesses to remain in that courtyard for the better part of an hour doing absolutely nothing, which the Census of Things in This City That Are Not Finished did not list, because Mira had not seen it, and Kael had seen it, and Kael did not write it down either, on the grounds that some entries belong to the people who have to live in them.

Mira walked the crack-mouths with chalk, marking which renovations were truly unfinished and which were bait. "Two of these alleys will be avenues by morning if we let them," she said. "We don't let them. Kael—ugly marks on the corners. Orphiel—blank pages pinned where forms will want to hang. Corvath—stand where the geometry gets lonely and tempt it into shame." "I can do shame," Corvath said. "I am fluent." Aureon cracked one more perfect stone at the avenue's lip and left the shovel's clay print like a signature. "If they polish this overnight, we crack it again. Maintenance of wounds. Bloom would approve." Veylan lingered as the others worked. "You understand the tower will only tighten its patience after this." "Patience is not virtue when it waits to close," Nahl said. "I learned that in a museum." "And if your doorstop vow gets people hurt?" "Then we heal uncleanly and keep the doors," Kael said, surprising himself with steel. "Hurt is not the same as filed. I'll take hurt." Veylan looked at Kael's scar, at Corvath's burn, at the fruit flies already discovering the sticky stones, and said nothing that could be notarized. When he left, he left by a crack, not by the avenue—a small cartography of doubt. Above the cracks, a flock of birds tried to form a grid, met Harmonix's off-beat clap echoing from a balcony, and broke into animal sky again. Gold weather stayed late, like a friend who refused to let the dark become a ledger.

chapters.part: Act III — The Road of Living Scars
chapters.label: Chapter 21
chapters.title: Mira Charts a Wound
paragraphs: After the ambush of perfect lines, Mira stopped drawing the city and started charting what the city had done to its own wounds. The safehouse listed like a drunk truth. They reached it by cracks and side courts, fruit still sticky on cloaks, Corvath's burn wrapped in Sancora's unclean poultice, Nahl's voice scraped thin from shouting doorstop into a white glove's patience.
